text: High-z Type Ia supernovae are expected to be gravitationally lensed by the foreground distribution of large-scale structure. The resulting magnification of supernovae is statistically measurable, and the angular correlation of the magnification pattern directly probes the integrated mass density along the line of sight. Measurements of cosmic magnification of supernovae therefore complements galaxy shear measurements in providing a direct measure of clustering of the dark matter. As the number of supernovae is typically much smaller than the number of sheared galaxies, the two-point correlation function of lensed Type Ia supernovae suffers from significantly increased shot noise. Neverthless, we find that the magnification map of a large sample of supernovae, such as that expected from next generation dedicated searches, will be easily measurable and provide an important cosmological tool. For example, a search over 20 sq. deg. over five years leading to a sample of ~ 10,000 supernovae would measure the angular power spectrum of cosmic magnification with a cumulative signal-to-noise ratio of ~20. This detection can be further improved once the supernova distance measurements are cross-correlated with measurements of the foreground galaxy distribution. The magnification maps made using supernovae can be used for important cross-checks with traditional lensing shear statistics obtained in the same fields, as well as help to control systematics. We discuss two applications of supernova magnification maps: the breaking of the mass-sheet degeneracy when estimating masses of shear-detected clusters, and constraining the second-order corrections to weak lensing observables.

High-z Type Ia supernovae are likely to be magnified by the mass of large-scale structures in front of them. This magnification can be measured statistically, and the pattern of this magnification helps us understand the total amount of mass along the line of sight. Studying how much these supernovae are magnified gives us another way to measure how dark matter is spread out in space. However, since there are far fewer supernovae than there are galaxies used for shear measurements, the pattern of magnification from supernovae is harder to see because of random noise. Still, with a large enough sample, like the ones we might find with future surveys, we can clearly measure the magnification pattern. For example, a survey covering 20 square degrees over five years, finding about 10,000 supernovae, could measure the pattern of magnification with a signal-to-noise ratio of about 20. This measurement can be even better if we compare the distances to the supernovae with the distribution of galaxies in front of them. These magnification maps can be compared to traditional lensing measurements in the same areas and help reduce errors. We look at two uses of these maps: helping to determine the mass of galaxy clusters more accurately and improving the accuracy of weak lensing measurements.

High-z Type Ia supernovae, those celestial fireworks exploding across the cosmos, are not immune to the gravitational pull of the large-scale structures lurking in their foreground. These cosmic giants are bent and magnified by the gravitational lensing effect of the universe’s invisible scaffolding—its dark matter web. The magnification they undergo is not random but forms a statistical pattern, one that reveals the accumulated mass density along the line of sight. This cosmic fingerprint, etched in the light of distant explosions, offers a complementary key to the puzzle of dark matter clustering, working alongside the more familiar galaxy shear measurements. Yet, with fewer supernovae in the sky than sheared galaxies, the two-point correlation function of these lensed beacons is plagued by a cacophony of shot noise. Still, when we peer into the future, where next-generation surveys will illuminate thousands of these stellar titans, the magnification map they carve into the heavens will be unmistakable—a cosmological compass. Imagine, over five years, a 20-square-degree survey yielding nearly 10,000 supernovae, each contributing to a magnification angular power spectrum with a signal-to-noise ratio of about 20. This beacon can be amplified further by weaving supernova distances with the distribution of foreground galaxies. These maps, forged in the light of exploding stars, will not only cross-check traditional lensing data but also help untangle the subtle systematics that haunt our understanding. They will break the mass-sheet degeneracy in cluster mass estimates and refine the second-order whispers of weak lensing.

We study a relativistic quantum cavity system realized by etching out from a graphene sheet by quantum transport measurements and theoretical calculations. The conductance of the graphene cavity has been measured as a function of the back gate voltage (or the Fermi energy) and the magnetic field applied perpendicular to the graphene sheet, and characteristic conductance contour patterns are observed in the measurements. In particular, two types of high conductance contour lines, i.e., straight and parabolic-like high conductance contour lines, are found in the measurements. The theoretical calculations are performed within the framework of tight-binding approach and Green's function formalism. Similar characteristic high conductance contour features as in the experiments are found in the calculations. The wave functions calculated at points selected along a straight conductance contour line are found to be dominated by a chain of scars of high probability distributions arranged as a necklace following the shape of cavity and the current density distributions calculated at these point are dominated by an overall vortex in the cavity. These characteristics are found to be insensitive to increasing magnetic field. However, the wave function probability distributions and the current density distributions calculated at points selected along a parabolic-like contour line show a clear dependence on increasing magnetic field, and the current density distributions at these points are characterized by the complex formation of several localized vortices in the cavity. Our work brings a new insight into quantum chaos in relativistic particle systems and would greatly stimulate experimental and theoretical efforts towards this still emerging field.

We investigate a relativistic quantum cavity system created by etching a region from a graphene sheet, using quantum transport measurements combined with theoretical calculations. The conductance of the graphene cavity has been measured in relation to the back gate voltage (or the Fermi energy) and the perpendicular magnetic field applied to the graphene sheet, revealing distinct conductance contour patterns. Specifically, two types of high conductance contour lines—straight and parabolic-like—are identified in the measurements. Theoretical calculations are conducted using the tight-binding approach and Green's function formalism. These calculations reproduce the characteristic high conductance contour features observed in the experiments. Wave functions calculated at points along a straight conductance contour line are predominantly influenced by a series of high probability distribution scars arranged in a necklace-like pattern following the cavity's shape, and the current density distributions at these points are dominated by a single vortex within the cavity. These features remain largely unchanged with increasing magnetic field. In contrast, wave function probability distributions and current density distributions calculated at points along a parabolic-like contour line demonstrate a clear dependence on increasing magnetic field, with current density distributions exhibiting multiple localized vortices. Our study provides new insights into quantum chaos in relativistic particle systems and may significantly encourage further experimental and theoretical research in this developing area.

We carve a relativistic quantum cavity from a graphene sheet, etching a stage for quantum drama, where transport measurements and theory conspire to unveil secrets. The conductance of this graphene stage is measured as the back gate voltage—akin to tuning a cosmic dial—and the perpendicular magnetic field twist the plot. From this, we carve out conductance contour maps, rich with character. Two distinct paths of high conductance emerge: one straight, like a blade of light, the other curving, like a whispering parabola. Theoretical models, built on tight-binding lattices and Green’s function sorcery, echo these experimental contours, mirroring the same high conductance trails. At points along the straight line, wave functions reveal a chain of scars, like a necklace of probability, clinging to the cavity's edge, while currents swirl in a grand vortex, unfazed by magnetic field’s growl. Yet, along the parabolic path, the story shifts. Here, probability and current dance to the magnetic field’s tune, birthing a tapestry of localized vortices, each a whirlpool of complexity. These findings, like a compass, guide us deeper into the realm of quantum chaos in relativistic systems, kindling fresh flames in both lab and mind, as this frontier of physics stretches its wings.

We investigate a relativistic quantum cavity system engineered through the etching of a graphene sheet, as revealed by quantum transport measurements and theoretical modeling. The conductance of this graphene cavity is measured as a function of back gate voltage—effectively modulating the Fermi energy—and the perpendicular magnetic field, resulting in distinctive conductance contour patterns. Two distinct types of high conductance contours emerge: one linear, the other parabolic in form. Theoretical analysis, grounded in tight-binding models and Green’s function formalism, replicates these experimental observations. Wave functions computed at points along the straight conductance contour exhibit a dominant configuration of high-probability scars arranged like a necklace, conforming to the cavity’s geometry, while current density distributions at these points display a singular vortex. These features remain largely invariant under increasing magnetic fields. In contrast, wave functions and current density distributions along parabolic-like contours reveal a marked sensitivity to magnetic field strength, manifesting in the formation of multiple localized vortices. These findings illuminate the complex interplay of quantum chaos within relativistic particle systems, offering a novel perspective that could catalyze both experimental and theoretical advancements in this nascent field.

The conductance of the graphene cavity has been measured in relation to the back gate voltage (or the Fermi energy) and the perpendicular magnetic field applied to the graphene sheet, revealing distinct conductance contour patterns. Specifically, two types of high conductance contour lines—straight and parabolic-like—are identified in the measurements. Theoretical calculations are conducted using the tight-binding approach and Green's function formalism. These calculations reproduce the characteristic high conductance contour features observed in the experiments. Wave functions calculated at points along a straight conductance contour line are predominantly influenced by a series of high probability distribution scars arranged in a necklace-like pattern following the cavity's shape, and the current density distributions at these points are dominated by a single vortex within the cavity. These features remain largely unchanged with increasing magnetic field. In contrast, wave function probability distributions and current density distributions calculated at points along a parabolic-like contour line demonstrate a clear dependence on increasing magnetic field, with current density distributions exhibiting multiple localized vortices. Our study provides new insights into quantum chaos in relativistic particle systems and may significantly encourage further experimental and theoretical research in this developing area.

The volume of discussions concerning brands within social media provides digital marketers with great opportunities for tracking and analyzing the feelings and views of consumers toward brands, products, influencers, services, and ad campaigns in CGC. The present study aims to assess and compare the performance of firms and celebrities (i.e., influencers that with the experience of being in an ad campaign of those companies) with the automated sentiment analysis that was employed for CGC at social media while exploring the feeling of the consumers toward them to observe which influencer (of two for each company) had a closer effect with the corresponding corporation on consumer minds. For this purpose, several consumer tweets from the pages of brands and influencers were utilized to make a comparison of machine learning and lexicon-based approaches to the sentiment analysis through the Naive algorithm (lexicon-based) and Naive Bayes algorithm (machine learning method) and obtain the desired results to assess the campaigns. The findings suggested that the approaches were dissimilar in terms of accuracy; the machine learning method yielded higher accuracy. Finally, the results showed which influencer was more appropriate according to their existence in previous campaigns and helped choose the right influencer in the future for our company and have a better, more appropriate, and more efficient ad campaign subsequently. It is required to conduct further studies on the accuracy improvement of the sentiment classification. This approach should be employed for other social media CGC types. The results revealed decision-making for which sentiment analysis methods are the best approaches for the analysis of social media. It was also found that companies should be aware of their consumers' sentiments and choose the right person every time they think of a campaign.

The extensive discourse on brands within social media platforms offers digital marketers a valuable opportunity to monitor and analyze consumer sentiments and perceptions regarding brands, products, influencers, services, and advertising campaigns in consumer-generated content (CGC). This study seeks to evaluate and compare the performance of companies and celebrities (i.e., influencers who have participated in advertising campaigns for these firms) using automated sentiment analysis techniques applied to CGC on social media. The objective is to explore consumer perceptions of these entities and determine which influencer, among two per company, had a more significant impact on consumer attitudes in alignment with the associated corporation. To achieve this, a sample of consumer tweets from brand and influencer pages was analyzed to compare machine learning and lexicon-based sentiment analysis approaches. Specifically, the Naive algorithm (lexicon-based) and the Naive Bayes algorithm (machine learning method) were used to evaluate the effectiveness of these approaches in assessing advertising campaigns. The results indicated differences in accuracy, with the machine learning method demonstrating higher precision. The study also identified the most suitable influencer based on their prior campaign involvement, thereby aiding in future influencer selection to enhance the effectiveness of advertising efforts. Further research is necessary to improve the accuracy of sentiment classification methods. This approach should be extended to other types of CGC on social media. The findings support the use of specific sentiment analysis methods for social media evaluation. It was also concluded that companies should monitor consumer sentiments and carefully select influencers for future campaigns.

The profusion of discourse surrounding brands on social media platforms presents digital marketers with an expansive terrain for tracking and analyzing consumer sentiment and perception toward brands, products, influencers, services, and advertising campaigns within the context of consumer-generated content (CGC). This study endeavors to evaluate and contrast the performance of firms and celebrities—specifically influencers who have previously participated in ad campaigns for these companies—by employing automated sentiment analysis techniques on CGC from social media, in order to gauge consumer sentiment and identify which of two selected influencers per company exerted a more congruent influence on consumer perception relative to the corresponding corporation. To achieve this, a corpus of consumer-generated tweets from brand and influencer pages was compiled, enabling a comparative analysis between machine learning and lexicon-based sentiment analysis approaches—specifically, the Naive algorithm (lexicon-based) and the Naive Bayes algorithm (machine learning method)—to derive insights regarding the effectiveness of ad campaigns. The findings revealed divergences in the accuracy of these approaches, with the machine learning method demonstrating superior precision. Ultimately, the results identified the influencer most aligned with the corporate brand in terms of consumer resonance, thereby offering strategic guidance for selecting optimal influencers in future campaigns. Further research is imperative to refine the accuracy of sentiment classification models, and this methodology should be extended to other forms of CGC across social media platforms. The study underscores the necessity for companies to remain attuned to consumer sentiment and to judiciously select influencers to maximize the efficacy of their advertising strategies.

Social media has become a big place for people to talk about brands, products, influencers, and ads. This gives digital marketers a chance to learn what people think and feel about these things. In this study, we looked at how well companies and their influencers did in campaigns by using automatic tools to check what people felt about them online. We compared two methods—machine learning and a word-based system—to see which gave better results.

We used tweets from brand and influencer pages to test these methods. The machine learning method, called Naive Bayes, performed better than the word-based one, called the Naive algorithm. Our results showed that one influencer from each company had a stronger connection with their audience, which helped us choose the best person for future campaigns.

We found that companies need to pay attention to what their customers feel and pick the right influencer for each campaign. This can make their ads more effective. More research is needed to improve how well these tools understand feelings. Also, this method could be used for other types of social media content. In the end, we learned which sentiment analysis method works best for understanding people's opinions online.

The digital cacophony of social media buzzes with brand chatter, offering marketers a goldmine of consumer sentiment, ripe for sifting and savoring. This study plunges into that chaos, seeking to measure how companies and their celebrity collaborators—those influencers who’ve danced in the spotlight of corporate ad campaigns—resonate with the public. It's a game of mirrors, reflecting which influencer, out of two per brand, casts the most authentic glow on the company’s image in the minds of consumers. To do this, we mined tweets from brand and influencer pages, using them as a lens to compare the sharpness of two sentiment analysis approaches: the lexicon-based Naive algorithm and the machine learning Naive Bayes method. The goal? To dissect the emotional undercurrents of these digital conversations and see which approach best captures the truth. The results were a revelation: the machine learning method, like a seasoned detective, unearthed higher accuracy. This insight illuminates the path forward, helping brands pick the right influencer for their next campaign, ensuring their message lands with precision and power. Yet, the quest isn’t over. Future work must sharpen the tools of sentiment classification, expanding their reach to other corners of social media. The study also whispers a warning: companies must tune into the emotional frequencies of their audience, for in that resonance lies the key to choosing the perfect collaborator, ensuring every campaign is not just seen, but felt.

It's a game of mirrors, reflecting which influencer, out of two per brand, casts the most authentic glow on the company’s image in the minds of consumers. To do this, we mined tweets from brand and influencer pages, using them as a lens to compare the sharpness of two sentiment analysis approaches: the lexicon-based Naive algorithm and the machine learning Naive Bayes method. The goal? To dissect the emotional undercurrents of these digital conversations and see which approach best captures the truth. The results were a revelation: the machine learning method, like a seasoned detective, unearthed higher accuracy. This insight illuminates the path forward, helping brands pick the right influencer for their next campaign, ensuring their message lands with precision and power. Yet, the quest isn’t over. Future work must sharpen the tools of sentiment classification, expanding their reach to other corners of social media. The study also whispers a warning: companies must tune into the emotional frequencies of their audience, for in that resonance lies the key to choosing the perfect collaborator, ensuring every campaign is not just seen, but felt.

Supervised machine learning methods usually require a large set of labeled examples for model training. However, in many real applications, there are plentiful unlabeled data but limited labeled data; and the acquisition of labels is costly. Active learning (AL) reduces the labeling cost by iteratively selecting the most valuable data to query their labels from the annotator. This article introduces a Python toobox ALiPy for active learning. ALiPy provides a module based implementation of active learning framework, which allows users to conveniently evaluate, compare and analyze the performance of active learning methods. In the toolbox, multiple options are available for each component of the learning framework, including data process, active selection, label query, results visualization, etc. In addition to the implementations of more than 20 state-of-the-art active learning algorithms, ALiPy also supports users to easily configure and implement their own approaches under different active learning settings, such as AL for multi-label data, AL with noisy annotators, AL with different costs and so on. The toolbox is well-documented and open-source on Github, and can be easily installed through PyPI.

Static properties of multiskyrmions with baryon numbers up to 8 are calculated, including momenta of inertia and sigma-term. The calculations are based on the recently suggested SU(2) rational map ansaetze. Minimization with the help of SU(3) variational minimization program shows that these configurations become local minima in SU(3) configuration space. The B-number dependence of the so called flavour moment of inertia of multiskyrmions playing an important role in the quantization procedure is close to the linear one. The spectra of baryonic systems with strangeness, charm and bottom are considered within a "rigid oscillator" version of the bound state soliton model. The binding energies estimates are made for the states with largest isospin which can appear as negatively charged nuclear fragments, as well as for states with zero isospin - light fragments of "flavoured" nuclear matter. Our results confirm the previously made observation that baryonic systems with charm or bottom quantum numbers have more chance to be stable with respect to strong interactions than strange baryonic systems.

In this paper, we consider sequential dynamic team decision problems with nonclassical information structures. First, we address the problem from the point of view of a "manager" who seeks to derive the optimal strategy of the team in a centralized process. We derive structural results that yield an information state for the team which does not depend on the control strategy, and thus it can lead to a dynamic programming decomposition where the optimization problem is over the space of the team's decisions. We, then, derive structural results for each team member that yield an information state which does not depend on their control strategy, and thus it can lead to a dynamic programming decomposition where the optimization problem for each team member is over the space of their decisions. Finally, we show that the control strategy of each team member is the same as the one derived by the manager. We present an illustrative example of a dynamic team with a delayed sharing information structure.

This paper examines sequential dynamic team decision problems characterized by nonclassical information structures. Initially, the problem is analyzed from the perspective of a "manager" aiming to determine the optimal strategy for the team through a centralized process. Structural results are derived that define an information state for the team, independent of the control strategy, thereby enabling a dynamic programming decomposition in which the optimization occurs over the team's decision space. Subsequently, structural results are established for each team member, defining an information state that is independent of their respective control strategy, facilitating a dynamic programming decomposition where each member's optimization problem is confined to their own decision space. Ultimately, it is demonstrated that the control strategy for each team member coincides with the one determined by the manager. An illustrative example of a dynamic team featuring a delayed sharing information structure is provided.

This paper looks at problems where a team makes decisions one after another, and where each member has different information. We start by thinking about how a manager might find the best overall strategy for the team as if they were making all the choices. We find a way to describe the team's situation that doesn't depend on the specific choices they make, which helps break the problem into smaller parts that can be solved step by step. Then, we look at each team member individually and find a similar way to describe their situation, again without depending on their choices. This lets us solve each person's part of the problem separately. In the end, we show that each person's best choice is the same as the one the manager would choose. We also give an example of a team that shares information with delays.

In this paper, we plunge into the murky waters of sequential dynamic team decision problems, where information flows are anything but classical. We begin by stepping into the shoes of a "manager," a puppeteer pulling strings to craft the team’s optimal strategy through a centralized lens. From this vantage, we carve out structural results that birth an information state—unshackled from the control strategy itself—allowing the team’s optimization to unravel like a thread through dynamic programming, weaving decisions into a coherent tapestry. Then, we turn our gaze inward, peeling back layers to reveal each team member's own information state, independent of their personal control strategy, granting them their own dynamic programming stage where decisions reign supreme. In the end, we unveil a surprising symmetry: each member’s control strategy mirrors the manager’s blueprint. To illustrate, we conjure a dynamic team navigating a delayed sharing information structure, a labyrinth where knowledge arrives not as a flood, but as a trickle.

We investigate the evolution of intracluster medium during a cluster merger, explicitly considering the relaxation process between the ions and electrons by N-body and hydrodynamical simulations. When two subclusters collide each other, a bow shock is formed between the centers of two substructures and propagate in both directions along the collision axis. The shock primarily heats the ions because the kinetic energy of an ion entering the shock is larger than that of an electron by the ratio of masses. In the post-shock region the energy is transported from the ions to electrons via Coulomb coupling. However, since the energy exchange timescale depends both on the gas density and temperature, distribution of electron temperature becomes more complex than that of the plasma mean temperature, especially in the expanding phase. After the collision of two subclusters, gas outflow occurs not only along the collision axis but also in its perpendicular direction. The gas which is originally located in the central part of the subclusters moves both in the parallel and perpendicular directions. Since the equilibrium timescale of the gas along these directions is relatively short, temperature difference between ions and electrons is larger in the directions tilted by the angles of $\pm 45^\circ$ with respect to the collision axis. The electron temperature could be significantly lower that the plasma mean temperature by $\sim 50 %$ at most. The significance of our results in the interpretation of X-ray observations is briefly discussed.

We plunge into the turbulent dance of the intracluster medium as two subclusters collide, their violent union unraveling the secrets of ion-electron relaxation through the lens of N-body and hydrodynamical simulations. When these galactic titans meet, a bow shock erupts between their cores, a fiery wave rippling outward along the collision axis like a thunderclap through the void. This shockwave, a titan in its own right, favors the ions—its fury more potent, its grip stronger, as the kinetic energy of ions dwarfs that of electrons by the sheer mass ratio. In the aftermath, the shock’s wrath is diffused, energy siphoned from ions to electrons via Coulomb coupling, but this transfer is no simple act—it is a slow, tangled negotiation, dependent on density and temperature, leaving electron temperatures in a state of complex disarray, especially as the gas swells in expansion. Gas does not merely flee along the collision axis; it spills outward in all directions, a cosmic deluge. The central gas, once anchored, now surges in parallel and perpendicular streams, a chaotic ballet. Yet, in this turbulence, equilibrium is swift along these paths, and so the temperature rift between ions and electrons grows most pronounced at angles of $\pm 45^\circ$ to the axis, where electrons may fall as much as half a degree below the mean plasma temperature. These findings, like a compass, guide our interpretation of X-ray whispers from the cosmos.

This shock predominantly heats the ions, as their kinetic energy upon entering the shock exceeds that of electrons by a factor corresponding to the mass ratio. We look at how the gas inside a galaxy cluster changes when two clusters collide, using computer models that track both the movement of particles and the flow of gas. When two smaller clusters crash into each other, a shock wave forms between them and spreads out in both directions along the line of the crash. This shock mainly heats the heavier particles, called ions, because they carry more energy than the lighter electrons when moving into the shock. After the shock passes, energy is slowly passed from ions to electrons through electric forces. But how fast this happens depends on how thick and hot the gas is, making the electron temperature more complicated than the average temperature of the gas, especially when the gas is spreading out. After the collision, gas flows out not just along the line of the crash, but also sideways. The gas that was in the center of each cluster moves both along and across the direction of the crash. Because the time it takes for the gas to balance out is shorter along these paths, the difference in temperature between ions and electrons is biggest in directions at about 45 degrees from the crash line. In these areas, the electrons can be as much as half as hot as the average temperature of the gas. We also briefly talk about how these findings might help explain what we see in X-ray images of galaxy clusters.

We look at how the gas inside a galaxy cluster changes when two clusters collide, using computer models that track both the movement of particles and the flow of gas. When two smaller clusters crash into each other, a shock wave forms between them and spreads out in both directions along the line of the crash. This shock mainly heats the heavier particles, called ions, because they carry more energy than the lighter electrons when moving into the shock. After the shock passes, energy is slowly passed from ions to electrons through electric forces. But how fast this happens depends on how thick and hot the gas is, making the electron temperature more complicated than the average temperature of the gas, especially when the gas is spreading out. After the collision, gas flows out not just along the line of the crash, but also sideways. The gas that was in the center of each cluster moves both along and across the direction of the crash. Because the time it takes for the gas to balance out is shorter along these paths, the difference in temperature between ions and electrons is biggest in directions at about 45 degrees from the crash line. In these areas, the electrons can be as much as half as hot as the average temperature of the gas. We also briefly talk about how these findings might help explain what we see in X-ray images of galaxy clusters.

We examine the transformation of the intracluster medium during the coalescence of galaxy clusters, with explicit attention to the relaxation dynamics between ions and electrons, as modeled through N-body and hydrodynamical simulations. Upon the collision of two subclusters, a bow shock emerges at the interface between the two substructures, propagating symmetrically along the collision axis. This shock predominantly heats the ions, as their kinetic energy upon entering the shock exceeds that of electrons by a factor corresponding to the mass ratio. In the post-shock domain, energy is transmitted from ions to electrons through Coulomb interactions. However, the timescale governing this energy exchange is contingent upon both the density and temperature of the gas, leading to a more intricate distribution of electron temperatures compared to the overall plasma temperature, particularly during the expansion phase. Following the collision, gas outflows manifest not only along the collision axis but also in transverse directions. The gas initially situated in the central regions of the subclusters migrates both parallel and perpendicular to the axis. Given the relatively brief equilibrium timescale along these axes, the disparity between ion and electron temperatures becomes more pronounced in directions inclined at angles of ±45° relative to the collision axis. Electron temperatures may fall as much as 50% below the plasma mean temperature. The implications of these findings for interpreting X-ray observations are briefly considered.

We plunge into the turbulent dance of the intracluster medium as two subclusters collide, their violent union unraveling the secrets of ion-electron relaxation through the lens of N-body and hydrodynamical simulations. When these galactic titans meet, a bow shock erupts between their cores, a fiery wave rippling outward along the collision axis like a thunderclap through the void. This shockwave, a titan in its own right, favors the ions—its fury more potent, its grip stronger, as the kinetic energy of ions dwarfs that of electrons by the sheer mass ratio. In the aftermath, the shock’s wrath is diffused, energy siphoned from ions to electrons via Coulomb coupling, but this transfer is no simple act—it is a slow, tangled negotiation, dependent on density and temperature, leaving electron temperatures in a state of complex disarray, especially as the gas swells in expansion. Gas does not merely flee along the collision axis; it spills outward in all directions, a cosmic deluge. The central gas, once anchored, now surges in parallel and perpendicular streams, a chaotic ballet. Yet, in this turbulence, equilibrium is swift along these paths, and so the temperature rift between ions and electrons grows most pronounced at angles of $\pm 45^\circ$ to the axis, where electrons may fall as much as half a degree below the mean plasma temperature. These findings, like a compass, guide our interpretation of X-ray whispers from the cosmos.

We investigate multi-spacecraft observations of the January 17, 2010 solar energetic particle event. Energetic electrons and protons have been observed over a remarkable large longitudinal range at the two STEREO spacecraft and SOHO suggesting a longitudinal spread of nearly 360 degrees at 1AU. The flaring active region, which was on the backside of the Sun as seen from Earth, was separated by more than 100 degrees in longitude from the magnetic footpoints of each of the three spacecraft. The event is characterized by strongly delayed energetic particle onsets with respect to the flare and only small or no anisotropies in the intensity measurements at all three locations. The presence of a coronal shock is evidenced by the observation of a type II radio burst from the Earth and STEREO B. In order to describe the observations in terms of particle transport in the interplanetary medium, including perpendicular diffusion, a 1D model describing the propagation along a magnetic field line (model 1) (Dr\"oge, 2003) and the 3D propagation model (model 2) by (Dr\"oge et al., 2010) including perpendicular diffusion in the interplanetary medium have been applied, respectively. While both models are capable of reproducing the observations, model 1 requires injection functions at the Sun of several hours. Model 2, which includes lateral transport in the solar wind, reveals high values for the ratio of perpendicular to parallel diffusion. Because we do not find evidence for unusual long injection functions at the Sun we favor a scenario with strong perpendicular transport in the interplanetary medium as explanation for the observations.

We examine multi-spacecraft data from the January 17, 2010 solar energetic particle event, where electrons and protons were observed across an extensive longitudinal span by the STEREO spacecraft and SOHO, indicating a near 360-degree spread at 1 AU. The source of the flare, situated on the solar far side relative to Earth, was longitudinally displaced by over 100 degrees from the magnetic footpoints of each of the three spacecraft. The event exhibits markedly delayed energetic particle arrivals compared to the initial flare, alongside minimal or absent anisotropies in intensity across all three vantage points. A coronal shock is inferred from the detection of a type II radio burst at both Earth and STEREO B. To interpret the data within the framework of interplanetary particle transport—incorporating perpendicular diffusion—we apply two models: a 1D model (model 1) by Dröge (2003), which traces propagation along magnetic field lines, and a 3D model (model 2) by Dröge et al. (2010), which accounts for lateral diffusion within the solar wind. While both models align with the observations, model 1 necessitates prolonged injection times at the Sun. Model 2, however, reveals substantial ratios of perpendicular to parallel diffusion. Since we find no evidence for extended injection periods, we posit that strong perpendicular transport within the interplanetary medium offers a more plausible explanation for the observed phenomena.

On January 17, 2010, we studied solar energetic particle observations from multiple spacecraft. Energetic electrons and protons were detected over a very wide area by the two STEREO spacecraft and SOHO, suggesting a spread of nearly 360 degrees at 1 AU. The active region that produced the flare was on the far side of the Sun from Earth, more than 100 degrees away in longitude from the magnetic footpoints of each of the three spacecraft. The event showed a strong delay between the flare and the arrival of energetic particles, with little or no directionality in the intensity measurements at all three locations. A coronal shock was likely present, as a type II radio burst was observed from Earth and STEREO B. To explain these observations, we used two models. One model described particle movement along a magnetic field line (model 1), and the other considered three-dimensional movement, including sideways diffusion in the solar wind (model 2). Both models matched the observations, but model 1 needed a long injection period from the Sun. Model 2, which includes sideways movement, showed that particles spread widely across the solar wind. Since we saw no signs of long injection times, we believe that strong sideways movement in the solar wind best explains the observations.

On the frost-kissed morning of January 17, 2010, the heavens erupted with a solar storm, casting its energy across the cosmos like a silent thunderclap. The STEREO spacecraft and SOHO, scattered like sentinels across the solar domain, bore witness to a spectacle of energetic electrons and protons, their trajectories stretching across a longitudinal expanse nearly encompassing the full circle of the sun's reign at 1 AU. The flare's source, a fiery wound on the sun's backside, lay far from the magnetic footprints of the three spacecraft, separated by over 100 degrees in longitude—a cosmic distance that whispered of unseen forces at play.

The particle onsets arrived late, like delayed echoes of a distant thunder, their timing lagging behind the flare’s initial scream. Yet the intensity measurements, devoid of sharp directional bias, hinted at a universe less ordered, more fluid. From Earth and STEREO B, a type II radio burst crackled through the void, a telltale sign of a coronal shock, like a ghostly hand reaching out from the sun’s corona.

To decode this celestial enigma, two models danced in the minds of researchers: one, a 1D journey along a magnetic thread; the other, a 3D ballet of particles weaving through the solar wind. Both could mimic the storm’s dance, yet the first demanded a prolonged injection of particles from the sun, stretching over hours. The second, embracing the lateral sprawl of the solar wind, unveiled a realm where perpendicular diffusion reigned supreme. With no evidence of such a long injection at the sun, the tale leans toward a universe where the interplanetary medium itself, not the sun, is the stage for this grand cosmic performance.

The second, embracing the lateral sprawl of the solar wind, unveiled a realm where perpendicular diffusion reigned supreme. With no evidence of such a long injection at the sun, the tale leans toward a universe where the interplanetary medium itself, not the sun, is the stage for this grand cosmic performance.

AIM: We have recently developed a microscopic Monte Carlo approach to study surface chemistry on interstellar grains and the morphology of ice mantles. The method is designed to eliminate the problems inherent in the rate-equation formalism to surface chemistry. Here we report the first use of this method in a chemical model of cold interstellar cloud cores that includes both gas-phase and surface chemistry. The surface chemical network consists of a small number of diffusive reactions that can produce molecular oxygen, water, carbon dioxide, formaldehyde, methanol and assorted radicals. METHOD: The simulation is started by running a gas-phase model including accretion onto grains but no surface chemistry or evaporation. The starting surface consists of either flat or rough olivine. We introduce the surface chemistry of the three species H, O and CO in an iterative manner using our stochastic technique. Under the conditions of the simulation, only atomic hydrogen can evaporate to a significant extent. Although it has little effect on other gas-phase species, the evaporation of atomic hydrogen changes its gas-phase abundance, which in turn changes the flux of atomic hydrogen onto grains. The effect on the surface chemistry is treated until convergence occurs. We neglect all non-thermal desorptive processes. RESULTS: We determine the mantle abundances of assorted molecules as a function of time through 2x10^5 yr. Our method also allows determination of the abundance of each molecule in specific monolayers. The mantle results can be compared with observations of water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and methanol ices in the sources W33A and Elias 16. Other than a slight underproduction of mantle CO, our results are in very good agreement with observations.

We recently created a microscopic Monte Carlo method to study how chemical reactions happen on the surfaces of interstellar dust grains and how ice layers form around them. This method avoids the problems that come with older methods used to study surface chemistry. In this work, we used this new method for the first time in a model of cold interstellar cloud cores, including both gas-phase and surface reactions. The surface reactions involve a few simple processes that can create molecules like molecular oxygen, water, carbon dioxide, formaldehyde, methanol, and various radicals.

The simulation starts by running a gas-phase model that includes the build-up of molecules on dust grains but no surface reactions or evaporation. The surface begins as either flat or rough olivine. We then gradually introduce surface reactions for hydrogen, oxygen, and carbon monoxide using our random method. In the simulation, only hydrogen atoms can evaporate in any meaningful amount. This affects the amount of hydrogen in the gas phase, which in turn changes how much hydrogen lands on the grains. We keep adjusting the surface chemistry until things settle down. We ignore any evaporation that isn’t caused by heat.

We track how much of each molecule is present in the ice layers over 200,000 years. Our method also tells us how much of each molecule is in specific layers of the ice. We compared our results with observations of water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and methanol ices in the sources W33A and Elias 16. The only exception is that we made a little less carbon monoxide ice than observed, but otherwise our results match the observations very well.

Our objective is to present a novel microscopic Monte Carlo framework designed to investigate interstellar surface chemistry and the structural evolution of ice mantles, circumventing the limitations of traditional rate-equation approaches. This study marks the inaugural application of this method within a chemical model of cold interstellar cloud cores, integrating both gas-phase and surface chemical processes. The surface chemical network comprises a limited set of diffusion-mediated reactions capable of synthesizing molecular oxygen, water, carbon dioxide, formaldehyde, methanol, and various radicals. The simulation is initialized by executing a gas-phase model that incorporates grain accretion but excludes surface chemistry and evaporation. The initial surface morphology is either flat or rough olivine. We sequentially introduce surface chemistry for hydrogen, oxygen, and carbon monoxide through an iterative stochastic procedure. Under the simulated conditions, only atomic hydrogen exhibits significant evaporation, an event that alters its gas-phase abundance and consequently modifies the flux of hydrogen atoms onto the grains. This feedback loop is iteratively resolved until convergence is achieved, while all non-thermal desorption mechanisms are omitted. By tracing molecular abundances within the ice mantle over a period of 2×10⁵ years, our methodology enables the determination of species distribution across individual monolayers. These results are corroborated by observational data from the sources W33A and Elias 16, concerning water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and methanol ices. The only notable discrepancy lies in the slightly diminished production of carbon monoxide within the mantle, while all other findings align closely with empirical measurements.

We've forged a microscopic Monte Carlo technique to probe the alchemy of surface chemistry on interstellar grains and the sculpting of ice mantles—like a painter’s brush on cosmic canvas. This method cuts through the knots and tangles of the rate-equation formalism, that old rigid framework. Now, we unveil the first deployment of this technique in a chemical model of cold interstellar cloud cores, where both gas-phase and surface reactions dance in tandem. The surface chemistry, a modest but potent network, involves a handful of diffusive reactions, each a step toward creating molecular oxygen, water, carbon dioxide, formaldehyde, methanol, and a gallery of radicals—each a whisper of complexity in the void.

We start by spinning a gas-phase model, letting molecules accrete onto grains, but keeping surface reactions and evaporation in abeyance. The initial surface? Either a smooth olivine or a rugged, pitted version. We introduce H, O, and CO onto the surface in an iterative, stochastic ballet. In the simulation’s cold, dark embrace, only atomic hydrogen dares to escape back into the gas phase, a flicker of rebellion. This escape subtly shifts its abundance in the gas, altering the stream of hydrogen raining down on the grains. We let this ripple through the surface chemistry until it settles into equilibrium. All non-thermal desorption? Left behind in the dust.

Through 200,000 years, we chart the mantle’s molecular abundance, layer by layer, a time-lapse of frost and chemistry. Our method peels back the layers, revealing the presence of each molecule in specific monolayers. These results, when compared to the ices of water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and methanol in the sources W33A and Elias 16, echo the observations closely—save for a faint murmur of underproduced CO, a small discord in the cosmic symphony.

The next generation of cosmology space missions will be sensitive to parasitic signals arising from cosmic rays. Using a composite bolometer, we have investigated pulses produced by $\alpha$ particles in order to understand the movement of energy produced by ionising radiation. Using a series of measurements at 100 mK, we have compared the typical fitting algorithm (a mathematical model) with a second method of pulse interpretation by convolving the detector's thermal response function with a starting profile of thermalised athermal phonons, taking into account the effects of heat propagation. Using this new fitting method, we have eliminated the need for a non-physical quadratic nonlinearity factor produced using more common methods, and we find a pulse form in good agreement with known aspects of thermal physics. This work is carried forward in the effort to produce a physical model for energy deposition in this detector. The modelling is motivated by the reproduction of statistical features in the experimental dataset, and the new interpretation of $\alpha$ pulse shapes represents an improvement in the current understanding of the energy propagation mechanisms in this detector.

This approach accounts for heat propagation effects. The newly developed fitting method removes the requirement for a non-physical quadratic nonlinearity factor typically used in standard methods. The resulting pulse form aligns closely with established principles of thermal physics. This research contributes to the development of a physical model for energy deposition within the detector. The modelling aims to replicate statistical features observed in the experimental dataset. The reinterpretation of $\alpha$ pulse shapes enhances the current understanding of energy propagation mechanisms within the detector.

We consider an index data structure for similar strings. The generalized suffix tree can be a solution for this. The generalized suffix tree of two strings $A$ and $B$ is a compacted trie representing all suffixes in $A$ and $B$. It has $|A|+|B|$ leaves and can be constructed in $O(|A|+|B|)$ time. However, if the two strings are similar, the generalized suffix tree is not efficient because it does not exploit the similarity which is usually represented as an alignment of $A$ and $B$. In this paper we propose a space/time-efficient suffix tree of alignment which wisely exploits the similarity in an alignment. Our suffix tree for an alignment of $A$ and $B$ has $|A| + l_d + l_1$ leaves where $l_d$ is the sum of the lengths of all parts of $B$ different from $A$ and $l_1$ is the sum of the lengths of some common parts of $A$ and $B$. We did not compromise the pattern search to reduce the space. Our suffix tree can be searched for a pattern $P$ in $O(|P|+occ)$ time where $occ$ is the number of occurrences of $P$ in $A$ and $B$. We also present an efficient algorithm to construct the suffix tree of alignment. When the suffix tree is constructed from scratch, the algorithm requires $O(|A| + l_d + l_1 + l_2)$ time where $l_2$ is the sum of the lengths of other common substrings of $A$ and $B$. When the suffix tree of $A$ is already given, it requires $O(l_d + l_1 + l_2)$ time.

We are looking at a way to organize information about similar strings. One possible method is the generalized suffix tree. This structure represents all the endings of two strings, A and B, in a compact way. It has as many end points as the total number of characters in A and B and can be built in a time proportional to the total length of both strings. However, when the two strings are very similar, this method isn't the most efficient. It doesn't use the similarity between the strings, which is often shown through an alignment of A and B. In this paper, we present a more efficient suffix tree that uses the alignment between A and B to save space and time. Our tree has a number of end points equal to the total length of A plus the sum of the lengths of the parts of B that differ from A, plus the sum of the lengths of some parts that are the same. We made sure not to sacrifice the ability to find patterns quickly while saving space. Searching for a pattern P in our tree takes time proportional to the length of P plus the number of times P appears in A and B. We also provide a fast method to build this tree. If we build it from scratch, it takes time proportional to the length of A, the sum of the different parts of B, the sum of some common parts, and the sum of other common parts. If we already have the suffix tree for A, it takes time proportional to the sum of the different parts, some common parts, and other common parts.

We propose an index structure tailored for strings exhibiting similarity, addressing the inefficiencies inherent in traditional generalized suffix trees. The generalized suffix tree, while capable of representing all suffixes of two strings $A$ and $B$ in a compacted trie with $|A|+|B|$ leaves, fails to capitalize on the structural redundancies that arise when $A$ and $B$ are aligned. This oversight diminishes its efficacy in scenarios where similarity is expressed through alignment. To resolve this, we introduce a suffix tree derived from an alignment of $A$ and $B$, strategically leveraging the shared structure to achieve a more refined spatial and temporal complexity. This alignment-based suffix tree features $|A| + l_d + l_1$ leaves, with $l_d$ denoting the cumulative length of segments in $B$ divergent from $A$, and $l_1$ representing the cumulative length of shared substrings between $A$ and $B$. Our design preserves the integrity of pattern search operations, allowing for a query time of $O(|P|+occ)$, where $occ$ denotes the count of occurrences of the pattern $P$ in both strings. Additionally, we present an algorithm for the construction of the alignment-based suffix tree, which demands $O(|A| + l_d + l_1 + l_2)$ time when built from scratch, with $l_2$ capturing the total length of other shared substrings. If the suffix tree of $A$ is already available, the construction time reduces to $O(l_d + l_1 + l_2)$.

Materials with coupled or competing order parameters display highly tunable ground states, where subtle perturbations reveal distinct electronic and magnetic phases. These phases generally are underpinned by complex crystal structures, but the role of structural complexity in these phases often is unclear. We use group theoretic methods and first-principles calculations to analyze a set of coupled structural distortions that underlie the polar charge- and orbitally- ordered antiferromagnetic ground state of $A$-site ordered SmBaMn$_2$O$_6$. We show that these distortions play a key role in establishing the ground state and stabilizing a network of domain wall vortices. Furthermore, we show that the crystal structure provides a knob to control competing electronic and magnetic phases at structural domain walls and in epitaxially strained thin films. These results provide new understanding of the complex physics realized across multiple length scales in SmBaMn$_2$O$_6$ and demonstrate a framework for systematic exploration of correlated and structurally complex materials.

Water drop impacting a superhydrophobic surface (SHS) rebounds completely with remarkable elasticity. For such an impact, the balance between the inertial and capillary forces ascertain the contact time. This is found to be fairly constant for any macroscopically flat SHS and for a given drop volume. Recently, various studies have shown that breaking the radial symmetry during the drop impact can significantly reduce the contact time below that of a flat SHS. One such study has been performed on a cylindrical SHS with a curvature comparable to the drop. The reduction in contact time has been attributed to the radially anisotropic flow imparted by the tangential component of momentum and the elliptical footprint of the drop during the crash. Here, we perform drop impact experiments on bathtub-like SHS and show that the radial anisotropy can be triggered even in the absence of both the criteria mentioned above. This is shown to be a consequence of the lamella deflection during the spreading of the drop. The reduction in contact time is quite clearly evident in this experimental regime.

A water drop slams onto a superhydrophobic surface, rebounds like a diamond skipping across glass, its bounce fueled by a strange, elastic vitality. The dance between inertia and capillary forces dictates how long it clings—this clinging time remains stubbornly consistent across any flat superhydrophobic stage, regardless of the drop's size. But when the drop's symmetry is shattered, the contact time plummets. One experiment, on a cylinder curved like a drop's own silhouette, revealed this secret: the drop's elliptical footprint and the swirling, directional push of its momentum twist the flow, shortening the embrace. Now, we've watched drops crash onto bathtub-shaped superhydrophobic surfaces, and even without the symmetry-breaking curve or the cylinder's curve, the drop still bends its path. The secret? As the drop spreads, its rim bends, deflecting the liquid's skin, and the contact time crumbles—evident, undeniable, and thrilling.

A water droplet striking a superhydrophobic surface rebounds with near-total elasticity, its dynamics governed by the equilibrium between inertial and capillary forces, which determine the contact duration. This duration remains largely invariant across any macroscopically flat superhydrophobic surface and for a given drop volume. Recent investigations reveal that disrupting radial symmetry during impact can drastically diminish the contact time below that of a flat surface. One such study employed a cylindrical superhydrophobic surface, whose curvature matched that of the drop, attributing the time reduction to radially anisotropic flow generated by the tangential momentum component and the elliptical footprint during impact. Here, we conduct experiments on bathtub-like superhydrophobic surfaces, demonstrating that radial anisotropy can be induced even without curvature matching or surface asymmetry. This phenomenon is traced to lamella deflection during spreading, resulting in a pronounced reduction in contact time within this experimental framework.

A water drop slams onto a superhydrophobic surface, rebounds like a diamond skipping across glass, its bounce fueled by a strange, elastic vitality. The dance between inertia and capillary forces dictates how long it clings—this clinging time remains stubbornly consistent across any flat superhydrophobic stage, regardless of the drop's size. But when the drop's symmetry is shattered, the contact time plummets. One experiment, on a cylinder curved like a drop's own silhouette, revealed this secret: the drop's elliptical footprint and the swirling, directional push of its momentum twist the flow, shortening the embrace. Now, we've watched drops crash onto bathtub-shaped superhydrophobic surfaces, and even without the symmetry-breaking curve or the cylinder's curve, the drop still bends its path. The secret? As the drop spreads, its rim bends, deflecting the liquid's skin, and the contact time crumbles—evident, undeniable, and thrilling.

For probabilistic programs, it is usually not possible to automatically derive exact information about their properties, such as the distribution of states at a given program point. Instead, one can attempt to derive approximations, such as upper bounds on tail probabilities. Such bounds can be obtained via concentration inequalities, which rely on the moments of a distribution, such as the expectation (the first raw moment) or the variance (the second central moment). Tail bounds obtained using central moments are often tighter than the ones obtained using raw moments, but automatically analyzing central moments is more challenging. This paper presents an analysis for probabilistic programs that automatically derives symbolic upper and lower bounds on variances, as well as higher central moments, of cost accumulators. To overcome the challenges of higher-moment analysis, it generalizes analyses for expectations with an algebraic abstraction that simultaneously analyzes different moments, utilizing relations between them. A key innovation is the notion of moment-polymorphic recursion, and a practical derivation system that handles recursive functions. The analysis has been implemented using a template-based technique that reduces the inference of polynomial bounds to linear programming. Experiments with our prototype central-moment analyzer show that, despite the analyzer's upper/lower bounds on various quantities, it obtains tighter tail bounds than an existing system that uses only raw moments, such as expectations.

For probabilistic programs, it is usually not possible to automatically find exact details about their behavior, like the spread of states at a certain point in the program. Instead, we try to find estimates, like limits on the chances of rare events. These limits can be found using mathematical tools that depend on features of a distribution, like average values or how much values vary around that average. Limits based on variation are often more precise than those based on average values alone, but analyzing variation is harder. This paper describes a method that automatically finds symbolic limits for variation and other related measures in programs that track costs. To handle the difficulty of analyzing these higher measures, the method uses a general approach that looks at different measures at the same time, taking advantage of how they relate. A major new idea is the concept of recursion that works for different measures, along with a system that can handle loops and repeated actions. The method uses a technique that turns the problem of finding bounds into a simpler math problem called linear programming. Testing with our system shows that even though it only gives upper and lower limits, it provides better estimates of rare events than a system that only uses average values.

O masters, lords, and rulers in all lands, Is this the handiwork you give to God, This monstrous thing distorted and soul-quenched? How will you ever straighten up this shape-; Touch it again with immortality; Give back the upward looking and the light; Rebuild in it the music and the dream; Make right the immemorial infamies, Perfidious wrongs, immedicable woes? But the real historic strength of England, physical and moral, has never had anything to do with this athletic specialism; it has been rather hindered by it. Somebody said that the Battle of Waterloo was won on Eton playing-fields. It was a particularly unfortunate remark, for the English contribution to the victory of Waterloo depended very much more than is common in victories upon the steadiness of the rank and file in an almost desperate situation. The Battle of Waterloo was won by the stubbornness of the common soldier—that is to say, it was won by the man who had never been to Eton. It was absurd to say that Waterloo was won on Eton cricket-fields. But it might have been fairly said that Waterloo was won on the village green, where clumsy boys played a very clumsy cricket. In a word, it was the average of the nation that was strong, and athletic glories do not indicate much about the average of a nation. Waterloo was not won by good cricket-players. But Waterloo was won by bad cricket-players, by a mass of men who had some minimum of athletic instincts and habits. It is a good sign in a nation when such things are done badly. It shows that all the people are doing them. And it is a bad sign in a nation when such things are done very well, for it shows that only a few experts and eccentrics are doing them, and that the nation is merely looking on. Suppose that whenever we heard of walking in England it always meant walking forty-five miles a day without fatigue. We should be perfectly certain that only a few men were walking at all, and that all the other British subjects were being wheeled about in Bath-chairs. But if when we hear of walking it means slow walking, painful walking, and frequent fatigue, then we know that the mass of the nation still is walking. We know that England is still literally on its feet.

The actual historical strength of England, both physically and morally, has never derived from its emphasis on athletic specialization. In fact, this focus has often impeded rather than enhanced national strength. A statement once made suggested that the Battle of Waterloo was won on the playing fields of Eton. This was an unfortunate assertion, as the English contribution to the Battle of Waterloo relied significantly on the steadfastness of ordinary soldiers in an extremely challenging and perilous situation. The Battle of Waterloo was ultimately secured by the perseverance of the common soldier—those who had never attended Eton. It was entirely inappropriate to claim that Waterloo was won on Eton's cricket fields. However, it could reasonably be said that the victory was achieved on the village green, where boys played an unrefined form of cricket. In summary, the strength of the nation lay in its average citizen, and athletic achievements do not necessarily reflect the general condition of a people. Waterloo was not won by accomplished cricketers, but by those who were not particularly skilled at the game. It was secured by a large group of individuals who possessed a basic level of athletic instinct and habit. It is a positive indicator for a nation when such activities are performed poorly, as it suggests that a broad segment of the population is engaged in them. Conversely, it is a negative sign when such activities are performed exceptionally well, because it implies that only a small group of specialists and outliers are involved, while the rest of the population merely observes. For example, if whenever we heard the word "walking" in England, it always referred to walking forty-five miles daily without tiring, we could be certain that only a small number of individuals were actually walking, while the rest of the British population remained confined to wheelchairs. However, if "walking" typically meant slow, painful, and tiring movement, we would know that the majority of the population was still walking. We would know that England, as a whole, was still literally on its feet.

But the true muscle and sinew of England, both in body and spirit, has never been found in the hallowed halls of athletic glory—it has often been shackled by it. Some fool once declared that the Battle of Waterloo was won on Eton's playing fields, a remark as glib as it was grotesque. For the English role in that battle hinged not on the prowess of the elite, but on the unyielding grit of the rank and file, pressed into a situation that reeked of despair. Waterloo was not conquered by the polished boots of Etonians, but by the stubborn hearts of those who had never set foot in a school that taught more about cricket than courage. It was absurd to suggest that Waterloo was won on Eton’s cricket fields. But it was not so absurd to imagine it was won on the village green, where lads fumbled with sticks and balls in a game as clumsy as their hands. In short, the strength of England lay in the average man, not in the athletic few. The glory of the cricket field tells us little of the soul of a nation. Waterloo was not won by those who played cricket well, but by those who played it poorly—by a sea of men with just enough of an athletic streak to keep them moving. It’s a good omen when such things are done badly, for it means the whole nation is at it. But when they’re done with flair, it means only a few are doing them, and the rest are watching from the sidelines. Imagine if every mention of walking in England meant men marching forty-five miles a day without a sigh. We’d know only a few were walking, and the rest were being pushed in Bath chairs. But if walking means a slow, aching trudge, then we know the whole nation is still on its feet, still moving, still alive.

But when walking is described as slow, arduous, and tiring, we discern that the populace as a whole is still on foot. We recognize that England, in its entirety, remains literally upon its feet.

The true historical fortitude of England, both corporeal and ethical, has never stemmed from its fixation upon athletic prowess; rather, this preoccupation has often obstructed its genuine strength. A statement once circulated that the Battle of Waterloo was secured on the cricket fields of Eton—a remark not only ill-conceived but deeply misleading. The English role in the triumph at Waterloo was not primarily the product of elite athleticism, but rather the resilience of the ordinary soldier, the steadfastness of the rank and file amidst near-catastrophic circumstances. Waterloo was not won by those who had attended Eton, but by the unrefined, unpolished common man, whose fortitude lay in his ordinariness. It was absurd to claim that Waterloo was decided on the manicured pitches of Eton. Yet, it might be said that the battle was won on the village green, where boys of limited grace played a game of equally limited skill. In essence, the strength of the nation lay in its average, and athletic distinction rarely reflects the average of a people. Waterloo was not conquered by those adept at cricket, but by those who were clumsy at it—by a multitude of individuals possessing only a rudimentary grasp of athleticism. It is a positive omen for a society when such pursuits are executed poorly, for it indicates that the entire populace engages in them. Conversely, when such endeavors are executed with mastery, it suggests that only a narrow segment of the population is involved, while the rest merely observe. Imagine if every mention of walking in England signified a forty-five-mile trek undertaken effortlessly—this would imply that only a few were walking, while the rest were confined to wheelchairs. But when walking is described as slow, arduous, and tiring, we discern that the populace as a whole is still on foot. We recognize that England, in its entirety, remains literally upon its feet.

But the true muscle and sinew of England, both in body and spirit, has never been found in the hallowed halls of athletic glory—it has often been shackled by it. Some fool once declared that the Battle of Waterloo was won on Eton's playing fields, a remark as glib as it was grotesque. For the English role in that battle hinged not on the prowess of the elite, but on the unyielding grit of the rank and file, pressed into a situation that reeked of despair. Waterloo was not conquered by the polished boots of Etonians, but by the stubborn hearts of those who had never set foot in a school that taught more about cricket than courage. It was absurd to suggest that Waterloo was won on Eton’s cricket fields. But it was not so absurd to imagine it was won on the village green, where lads fumbled with sticks and balls in a game as clumsy as their hands. In short, the strength of England lay in the average man, not in the athletic few. The glory of the cricket field tells us little of the soul of a nation. Waterloo was not won by those who played cricket well, but by those who played it poorly—by a sea of men with just enough of an athletic streak to keep them moving. It’s a good omen when such things are done badly, for it means the whole nation is at it. But when they’re done with flair, it means only a few are doing them, and the rest are watching from the sidelines. Imagine if every mention of walking in England meant men marching forty-five miles a day without a sigh. We’d know only a few were walking, and the rest were being pushed in Bath chairs. But if walking means a slow, aching trudge, then we know the whole nation is still on its feet, still moving, still alive.

Neither make too much of flaws and occasional overstatements. Some persons seem to think that absolute truth, in the form of rigidly stated propositions, is all that conversation admits. This is precisely as if a musician should insist on having nothing but perfect chords and simple melodies,—no diminished fifths, no flat sevenths, no flourishes, on any account. Now it is fair to say, that, just as music must have all these, so conversation must have its partial truths, its embellished truths, its exaggerated truths. It is in its higher forms an artistic product, and admits the ideal element as much as pictures or statues. One man who is a little too literal can spoil the talk of a whole tableful of men of *esprit*.—"Yes," you say, "but who wants to hear fanciful people's nonsense? Put the facts to it, and then see where it is!"—Certainly, if a man is too fond of paradox,—if he is flighty and empty,—if, instead of striking those fifths and sevenths, those harmonious discords, often so much better than the twinned octaves, in the music of thought,—if, instead of striking these, he jangles the chords, stick a fact into him like a stiletto. But remember that talking is one of the fine arts,—the noblest, the most important, and the most difficult,—and that its fluent harmonies may be spoiled by the intrusion of a single harsh note. Therefore conversation which is suggestive rather than argumentative, which lets out the most of each talker's results of thought, is commonly the pleasantest and the most profitable. It is not easy, at the best, for two persons talking together to make the most of each other's thoughts, there are so many of them.

Do not overestimate the significance of imperfections or the occasional hyperbolic assertion. Some individuals mistakenly believe that conversation is confined solely to the domain of absolute, rigidly articulated truths, as though a musician could compose only with flawless chords and unadorned melodies, excluding all diminished fifths, flat sevenths, or embellishing flourishes. Yet just as music derives its richness from such dissonances and ornamentations, so too does dialogue thrive upon partial truths, embellished truths, and even exaggerated ones. In its more elevated forms, conversation is an artistic endeavor, as capable of embodying ideal elements as are paintings or sculptures. A single individual, overly literal in his speech, may disrupt the entire discourse of a gathering of intellectually agile minds. “But,” one might object, “who desires to hear the whimsical ramblings of fanciful individuals? Let facts govern the discussion.” Indeed, if a speaker is overly inclined toward paradox, if he is capricious and hollow, if he fails to strike those dissonant yet harmonious intervals—those fifth and seventh chords, so often more evocative than the simple octaves of thought—and instead merely jangles the chords, then a fact thrust into his discourse is like a stiletto to the ribs. Yet recall that conversation is among the most refined, significant, and challenging of the fine arts, and a single discordant note may spoil the flowing harmonies of discourse. Thus, the most agreeable and beneficial conversations are those that are suggestive rather than combative, allowing each participant’s reflections to emerge fully. It is rarely easy for two individuals to fully illuminate one another’s thoughts, given the sheer volume of ideas each carries.

A single stiff, literalist can unravel the entire weave of a table's discourse, like a thread snapping in a tapestry of wit. “But,” you protest, “who wants to listen to a man who’s all smoke and no fire? Give me the facts, and let’s see where he stands!”—True, if a speaker is a mere windbag, if he flits from idea to idea, never hitting the right chord, never letting the dissonances sing—then indeed, a fact can be thrust into him like a dagger. Yet recall: conversation is among the grand arts, the most refined, the most demanding, the most delicate. One sour note can fracture a whole melody. Thus, the best talk is not about winning arguments but about sharing the glow of thought, letting each voice cast light on the others’ minds. It is rare, though, for two people to truly pull the best from each other’s thoughts—so many ideas, so little time.
