Then there are the sentimentalists, who are the largest class and who make the easiest work of social questions. In the study of the individual organism we know that normal physiology presents the greatest difficulties and is the essential basis for a correct study of diseases and remedies. We also know that popular knowledge of physiology is meager in the extreme, while popular notions attach almost entirely to diseases and to remedies. The same is true of society. The study of the structure and functions of the organs of society is long and difficult, and we have, as yet, accomplished very little towards it. We can hope to accomplish much only by a long study of history and a careful examination of institutions. I venture to say that no study except the highest mathematics has ever yet made such demands on the human mind as are made by sociology. We cannot make an experiment in sociology because we cannot dispose of the time, that is, of the lives of a body of men and women. We have to carry in mind a great number of variables, to weigh their value, and to deduce their resultant, although for many of them we can find no unit of measurement or comparison, and although we have no notation to help us. I think that we shall have to adopt some of these methods of the other sciences sooner or later, but at present I see no means of advancing sociology save by the cultivation of a trained judgment through the careful study of sociological phenomena and sequences.

Then there are the sentimentalists, who constitute the largest group and who approach social issues with the least difficulty. In the study of the individual organism, we recognize that normal physiology presents the greatest challenges and serves as the fundamental basis for understanding diseases and treatments. We also recognize that general knowledge of physiology is extremely limited, while popular understanding is largely focused on diseases and their cures. The same pattern applies to society. Investigating the structure and functions of societal institutions is lengthy and complex, and we have achieved very little in this regard. Progress requires extensive historical study and detailed examination of existing institutions. I assert that no discipline, except for the highest mathematics, has imposed such rigorous demands on the human mind as sociology. In sociology, experimentation is not feasible because we cannot manipulate time, that is, the lives of individuals. We must consider numerous variables, assess their significance, and determine their combined effects, even though many lack standardized units of measurement or comparison and no formal notation exists to assist us. I believe that eventually we will need to adopt some methods used in other sciences, but for now, I see no alternative to advancing sociology except through the development of trained judgment via careful study of sociological phenomena and their sequences.

I suspect we’ll eventually borrow tools from other sciences, but for now, the only way forward is to sharpen our judgment through the patient observation of social patterns and their unfolding consequences.

When we look at the human body, we see that understanding normal functions is the hardest part and the key to learning about diseases and treatments. People know very little about how the body works, but they know a lot about sickness and cures. It's the same with society. Learning about how society is built and how it works is slow and hard, and we've barely made progress. We can only learn a lot by studying history and looking closely at institutions. I believe that no field, except maybe the highest math, has ever needed as much from the human mind as sociology does. We can't do experiments in sociology because we can't control time—meaning the lives of people. We must keep track of many different factors, decide how important they are, and figure out the outcome, even though we often can't measure or compare them, and we have no way to write them down. I think we'll eventually use some methods from other sciences, but right now, the only way to move forward is to develop good judgment by carefully studying social events and how they follow each other.

President Lincoln in a note to Mayor Ramsey once wrote: "The lady bearer of this note says she has two sons who want to work. Set them at it if possible. Wanting work is so rare a want that it should be encouraged." A college officer in my position at the opening of the college year would not be inclined to agree with Mr. Lincoln, for half the correspondence which comes to my desk during the summer months has to do with men who either want to work, or who say they do, in order that they may defray their college expenses. There are so many of them that their correspondence becomes almost depressing at times, for I realize the disappointments and the difficulties which very many of these boys will encounter after they reach college, and their unfitness to do any definite work well. "I have been out of high school three years," one young fellow writes, "and have not been able to save any money. I want, however, very much to go to college. Can you secure a place for me to work where I can earn my board and room and such extra money as I shall need for my other small expenses?" This man, who has given all his time to work for three years and who has done nothing more than live, expects easily to carry a college course which in itself requires most of a man's time to do justice to, and at the same time to earn his living on the side. I get many such letters from those who feel that earning one's living and going to college are in no way incompatible. So much has been written about the fellows who have started to college without a cent and who have later been valedictorians of their classes and ultimately President of the United States, or at least a member of his cabinet, that the average high school boy has little conception of what sacrifice and deprivation such a procedure involves; if he did understand he would nat so often undertake it, or he would do so after more careful deliberation.

The desire for work is so rare that it should be encouraged." A college administrator in my position at the beginning of the academic year would not concur with Mr. Lincoln, as half the correspondence received during the summer months concerns men who either seek work or claim to in order to cover their college expenses. Can you find me a position where I can earn my board, lodging, and additional funds for my other expenses?" This young man, who has spent the past three years working and nothing else, expects to successfully complete a college curriculum, which itself demands a significant portion of a person’s time, while simultaneously earning a living. As a result, the average high school student has little understanding of the sacrifice and hardship involved in such a path. If he did understand, he would not so frequently pursue it, or he would do so following more deliberate consideration.

President Lincoln once scribbled a note to Mayor Ramsey, saying something like: "The woman carrying this note claims she has two sons eager to work. Put them to it if you can. The desire to work is a rare and precious thing—nurture it." But here I am, a college officer, at the cusp of the academic year, and I find myself at odds with Lincoln’s sentiment. Half the letters that flood my desk in the summer months are from young men—some say they want to work, others just say they do—because they need to pay for college. It’s a deluge, and it weighs on the soul. I see the struggle in their words, the unspoken fears of failure, the blind spots of their own unpreparedness. One kid writes, “I’ve been out of high school three years, and I haven’t saved a dime. But I want to go to college. Can you find me a place to work where I can earn my board, my room, and a little extra for other expenses?” This guy, who’s spent those three years working and living, thinks he can somehow juggle a full college course—something that demands every ounce of a man’s energy—and still make ends meet on the side. I get letters like this all the time, from boys who think earning a living and going to college are two halves of the same coin. There are stories—tales of those who started with nothing, became valedictorians, then presidents or cabinet members—that warp the reality of what it takes. These stories paint a picture of triumph without the shadow of sacrifice. The average high school boy doesn’t grasp the weight of that journey, the deprivation, the silent suffering. If he did, he wouldn’t leap into it so often, or he’d think twice, plan better, and not charge ahead with blind courage.

One individual writes: "I have been out of high school for three years and have not been able to save any money. I very much wish to attend college. Can you find me a position where I can earn my board, lodging, and additional funds for my other expenses?" This young man, who has spent the past three years working and nothing else, expects to successfully complete a college curriculum, which itself demands a significant portion of a person’s time, while simultaneously earning a living. I receive numerous such letters from individuals who believe that working to support oneself and attending college are not mutually exclusive. Much has been written about students who began college with no financial resources and later became valedictorians of their classes, eventually becoming President of the United States or at least a member of his cabinet. As a result, the average high school student has little understanding of the sacrifice and hardship involved in such a path. If he did understand, he would not so frequently pursue it, or he would do so following more deliberate consideration.

President Lincoln, in a letter to Mayor Ramsey, once observed: "The lady who bears this note mentions that she has two sons desiring employment. Provide them with such opportunities if feasible. The desire for labor is an anomaly so rare that it warrants cultivation." A college administrator in my position, at the onset of the academic year, would likely find himself at odds with this sentiment, for a significant portion of the correspondence that accumulates on my desk during the summer months pertains to young men who either express a desire for work or feign one, primarily to subsidize their college costs. The sheer volume of these letters often evokes a sense of despondency, for I am acutely aware of the disappointments and obstacles that many of these individuals will face upon entering college, compounded by their evident lack of preparedness to perform any specific task with proficiency. One young man writes: "I have been away from high school for three years and have not managed to save any money. Nevertheless, I am very eager to attend college. Might you be able to secure for me a position where I might earn my board, lodging, and a modest stipend for my other expenses?" This individual, who has spent three years entirely in pursuit of sustenance, expects with ease to manage a rigorous college curriculum—which alone demands the bulk of one's energy—and simultaneously to sustain himself financially. I receive numerous such letters from individuals who perceive earning a living and pursuing higher education as mutually compatible pursuits. Much has been chronicled regarding those who commenced their college journey with nothing but ambition, only to emerge as valedictorians or even ascend to positions of national leadership, or at the very least, to serve in their cabinets. Consequently, the average high school student harbors a limited understanding of the magnitude of sacrifice and deprivation such an endeavor entails; should they grasp its true nature, they would less frequently embark upon it, or do so only after a more deliberate and measured contemplation.

President Lincoln once scribbled a note to Mayor Ramsey, saying something like: "The woman carrying this note claims she has two sons eager to work. Put them to it if you can. The desire to work is a rare and precious thing—nurture it." But here I am, a college officer, at the cusp of the academic year, and I find myself at odds with Lincoln’s sentiment. Half the letters that flood my desk in the summer months are from young men—some say they want to work, others just say they do—because they need to pay for college. It’s a deluge, and it weighs on the soul. I see the struggle in their words, the unspoken fears of failure, the blind spots of their own unpreparedness. One kid writes, “I’ve been out of high school three years, and I haven’t saved a dime. But I want to go to college. Can you find me a place to work where I can earn my board, my room, and a little extra for other expenses?” This guy, who’s spent those three years working and living, thinks he can somehow juggle a full college course—something that demands every ounce of a man’s energy—and still make ends meet on the side. I get letters like this all the time, from boys who think earning a living and going to college are two halves of the same coin. There are stories—tales of those who started with nothing, became valedictorians, then presidents or cabinet members—that warp the reality of what it takes. These stories paint a picture of triumph without the shadow of sacrifice. The average high school boy doesn’t grasp the weight of that journey, the deprivation, the silent suffering. If he did, he wouldn’t leap into it so often, or he’d think twice, plan better, and not charge ahead with blind courage.

But, although palæontology is a comparatively youthful scientific speciality, the mass of materials with which it has to deal is already prodigious. In the last fifty years the number of known fossil remains of invertebrated animals has been trebled or quadrupled. The work of interpretation of vertebrate fossils, the foundations of which were so solidly laid by Cuvier, was carried on, with wonderful vigour and success, by Agassiz in Switzerland, by Von Meyer in Germany, and last, but not least, by Owen in this country, while, in later years, a multitude of workers have laboured in the same field. In many groups of the animal kingdom the number of fossil forms already known is as great as that of the existing species. In some cases it is much greater; and there are entire orders of animals of the existence of which we should know nothing except for the evidence afforded by fossil remains. With all this it may be safely assumed that, at the present moment, we are not acquainted with a tithe of the fossils which will sooner or later be discovered. If we may judge by the profusion yielded within the last few years by the Tertiary formations of North America, there seems to be no limit to the multitude of Mammalian remains to be expected from that continent; and analogy leads us to expect similar riches in Eastern Asia, whenever the Tertiary formations of that region are as carefully explored. Again, we have as yet almost everything to learn respecting the terrestrial population of the Mesozoic epoch—and it seems as if the Western territories of the United States were about to prove as instructive in regard to this point as they have in respect of tertiary life. My friend Professor Marsh informs me that, within two years, remains of more than 160 distinct individuals of mammals, belonging to twenty species and nine genera, have been found in a space not larger than the floor of a good-sized room; while beds of the same age have yielded 300 reptiles, varying in size from a length of 60 feet or 80 feet to the dimensions of a rabbit.

Although palaeontology is a relatively young scientific discipline, the volume of material it examines is already immense. Over the past fifty years, the number of known fossil remains of invertebrate animals has increased three- or fourfold. The study of vertebrate fossils, which was firmly established by Cuvier, was continued with remarkable energy and success by Agassiz in Switzerland, by Von Meyer in Germany, and, not least, by Owen in this country. In more recent years, numerous researchers have continued this work in the same field. In many animal groups, the number of known fossil species is as large as the number of currently existing species. In some instances, it is even greater. Entire animal orders would be unknown to us were it not for the evidence provided by fossil remains. Despite this, it is reasonable to assume that we are currently aware of only a small fraction of the fossils that will eventually be discovered. Judging by the abundance of fossils recently uncovered in the Tertiary formations of North America, there appears to be no limit to the number of mammalian remains that may be found on that continent. By analogy, similar richness may be expected in Eastern Asia once its Tertiary formations are thoroughly explored. Furthermore, our knowledge of the terrestrial life of the Mesozoic era remains largely incomplete. It appears that the western territories of the United States may provide as much insight into this period as they have regarding Tertiary life. Over the past half-century, the number of identified fossil remains of invertebrate animals has tripled or even quadrupled. The interpretation of vertebrate fossils, a field firmly established by Cuvier, was further advanced with remarkable energy and success by Agassiz in Switzerland, by Von Meyer in Germany, and, not least, by Owen in this country. In more recent times, a multitude of scholars have continued this work within the same domain. In numerous segments of the animal kingdom, the number of known fossil species equals or even surpasses that of living species. In certain cases, the fossil record is substantially more extensive; indeed, entire orders of animals would remain entirely unknown to us were it not for the evidence preserved in the fossil record. Despite this, it is reasonable to assume that we are currently aware of only a fraction of the fossils that will eventually be unearthed. Judging from the recent abundance of fossils uncovered in the Tertiary formations of North America, it appears there is no upper bound to the number of mammalian remains yet to be discovered from that continent; analogical reasoning suggests similar richness may await in Eastern Asia, once its Tertiary strata are subjected to thorough investigation. Moreover, our understanding of the terrestrial fauna of the Mesozoic era remains largely incomplete, and it seems the western territories of the United States may yet prove as enlightening in this regard as they have been concerning Tertiary life. Paleontology, though a young science, wrestles with a mountain of bones and dust—so vast it seems the earth itself is coughing up its ancient secrets. In half a century, the fossilized remnants of invertebrates have tripled or quadrupled, a deluge of shells and skeletons buried deep in time. The deciphering of vertebrate fossils, a task first laid with iron precision by Cuvier, has since been carved into the bedrock of discovery by Agassiz in the Swiss Alps, by Von Meyer in German lands, and by Owen here in our own isle. And now, a host of others, like a tide of scholars, have surged into this realm of buried truths.

In many branches of the animal kingdom, the number of known fossils rivals the living species that walk, swim, and flutter today. In some cases, the dead outnumber the living—entire orders of creatures, whose names we would never know, if not for the whispers of their bones. And yet, for all this, we are but scratching the surface. The Tertiary layers of North America, in recent years, have spilled forth a cornucopia of mammals, hinting at a trove of remains yet to be unearthed. By analogy, the same bounty may await in the hidden folds of Eastern Asia, should its Tertiary strata be given the same careful attention.

And what of the Mesozoic? The terrestrial world of that age remains a vast enigma, but the Western territories of the United States seem poised to offer revelations as profound as those they’ve already given of the Tertiary. Professor Marsh has told me that within two years, more than 160 mammalian remains—spanning twenty species and nine genera—were uncovered in a space no larger than a room’s floor. From the same strata, 300 reptiles emerged, some the size of a house, others no bigger than a rabbit, as if the earth had cradled a menagerie of giants and gnomes in its ancient depths.

Cross-examined.—I am an officer in the Grenadier Guards. I have had some experience of stage-plays. I believe that nothing is easier than to write a good stage-play. I have written one myself. I found it extremely easy. Mounting guard was an intellectual exercise not to be mentioned in the same breath with it. My play has not been produced—not yet. I have shown it to several managers—they hesitate to produce it, on the ground that it is too intellectual. I had no objection to bring it down to the comprehension of the audience; but I did not see any way of making it less intellectual than it was—I have no objection to state its name—it is a burlesque called *Tom Tiddler.*

Cross-examined.—I serve as an officer within the Grenadier Guards, a role that has afforded me some acquaintance with the theatrical arts. I hold the conviction that composing a successful stage-play demands little more than a modicum of ingenuity. I myself have authored one, a task I found deceptively simple, rendering the complexities of mounting guard a mere shadow in comparison. My work, however, remains unproduced, its potential unrealized. I have presented it to various theatrical managers, who have balked at its production, citing its excessive intellectualism. I have no quarrel with simplifying it for the audience’s grasp, yet I perceive no viable path to diminishing its intellectual rigor. The title, if I may disclose it, is a burlesque entitled *Tom Tiddler.*

Cross-examined.—I am a Grenadier Guardsman, a man of discipline and decorum, yet I’ve dabbled in the theatre’s wild, flickering world. I’ve found the art of stagecraft simpler than the rigid ritual of mounting guard—truly, a mere child’s game compared to the solemnity of duty. I penned a play myself, a burlesque titled *Tom Tiddler*, and it flowed from me like a river unchained. Yet, though I’ve shown it to the theatre’s gatekeepers, they’ve balked, calling it too cerebral, too sharp for the common ear. I’d gladly dumb it down, but how does one strip a play of its mind? It is what it is—too bright for the dim glow of the stage, perhaps.

The young man with the buoyancy and optimism of Mr. Skimpole, in *[Bleak House](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Bleak_House),* who held that "the sordid word money should never be mentioned in the relations of friendship" is having little vogue at the present time. The enthusiastic life insurance agent, if you will admit his logic, can prove to you that if you will pay your premiums long enough they will cost you nothing, but every sensible man knows that the thing that is worth anything costs something, and the fraternity is no exception. Fraternity men in the past have too frequently taken their obligations lightly, and so in a financial way have brought fraternities into disrepute. Fraternity officers have begun strongly to emphasize the importance of financial matters in the fraternity and are insisting upon the introduction of accounting systems into all chapters which will make it possible for fraternity accounts to be kept accurately and which will impress upon the fraternity man from the outset his obligation to meet his bills when they are due. When a boy goes into a fraternity, neither he nor his father should be deceived as to the actual cost of membership, nor allowed to believe that payment may be evaded or deferred. It is ordinarily as unwise to go into a fraternity with the idea that the cost of living will thus be reduced as it is to enter matrimony with the thought that it will cost no more to support a family than an individual. With us at the University of Illinois the fraternity man is likely to be called upon to expend twenty per cent more than if he had remained outside of the organization, and if he develops popularity and contracts the joining habit, it may cost him considerably more than this.

Merited and timely as such criticism may appear to a transient observer of the State university, it is recognized as superficial and essentially false by all those who have felt the inner throb and glow of the enterprise. Idealist the institution is not, if idealism means a sterile yearning for the unattainable. Materialist it is not, if materialism is identified with satisfaction in the welfare of the senses. The State university to-day is at the same time intensely visionary and intensely practical: its driving power is the creative artist's desire to externalize and eternize his dream. With eyes fixed upon that end, it does not shrink from the coarse tasks of mixing pigments, quarrying stone, or melting bronze. It would honor every truth by use, and it holds that the triumph of the spiritual is the subjugation of the material. The financial support which it solicits is the means to the realization of a vision embracing almost the whole of life, and the wealth which it helps to create is but the first fruits of its contemplated harvest.

Though the criticism of the State university may seem merited and timely to an outsider, those intimately familiar with its operations regard it as superficial and fundamentally incorrect. The institution is neither idealist in the sense of pursuing an unattainable and sterile vision, nor materialist in the sense of seeking only sensory gratification. Contemporary State universities are simultaneously deeply visionary and profoundly practical. Their motivation arises from the creative artist's impulse to externalize and preserve his vision. With this objective in view, they do not avoid the laborious tasks of pigment mixing, stone quarrying, or metal melting. They value truth only when it is applied, believing that the triumph of the spiritual lies in the mastery of the material. The financial support they seek serves as a means to achieve a vision that encompasses nearly all aspects of life, and the wealth they help generate is merely the initial yield of a broader harvest they intend to realize.

The funds it seeks are but tools for a grand vision that touches nearly every corner of life, and the riches it helps forge are but the first ripe fruit of a much greater yield.

The preeminence of our most distinguished comic dramatist rests upon no more than three of his five plays, each a crystallization of the form’s essence. His initial foray into comedy was but a refined imitation of models that his own earliest work would ultimately eclipse; and when he turned to tragedy, his handling of it bore the artifice and affectation of Lady Wishfort’s cosmetics—superficially adorned, yet marked by the cracks of inauthenticity. Yet his three seminal comedies alone suffice to establish a legacy as enduring as the language itself. Without them, we would lack exemplars of comedy in its most refined and elevated manifestation. Ben Jonson, the lone figure who sought to reform the theatrical landscape by isolating comedy from the tangled fusion of tragedy and comedy that characterized the stage of his era—a fusion as entwined as life itself—nevertheless failed to imbue his intricate and grand designs with the fluidity and elegance intrinsic to the comic spirit. Among Congreve’s immediate predecessors, who endeavored to construct a new English comedy upon French foundations, Wycherley’s work was of a base alloy, while Etherege’s was too insubstantial to compare. No other contemporaries offered anything beyond the crude, unrefined ore of Shadwell’s coarse and unadorned talent. Drawing from Landor, we might assert that a single limb of Molière would have sufficed to forge a Congreve, and conversely, a limb of Congreve would have been enough to shape a Sheridan. The vigorous and expansive humor of Vanbrugh’s comedies, though admirable, secures him a place in the company of the master, though not as his equal.

The glory of our greatest comic dramatist is built upon, or nearly built upon, only three of his five plays. His first comedy was but a dazzling echo of models that his own early work would later eclipse, a pale imitation that paled before the brilliance of its imitator. His tragedies, meanwhile, are like a painted face—rouged, wrinkled, and patched, like Lady Wishfort herself, trying to disguise the cracks beneath. But those three great comedies of his? They are more than enough to carve a reputation as enduring as our very language. Without them, we’d have no true samples of comedy in its purest, most exalted form.

Ben Jonson, the lone soul who sought to reform comedy amid the muddled chaos of a time when tragedy and comedy were as tangled on stage as they were in life, failed to grant his grand and elaborate work the effortless grace and the fluid motion that comic life demands. He tried, but his work remained too stiff, too ponderous, like a fine suit made from the wrong cloth.

Of Congreve’s immediate predecessors, those who had aimed to build a new English comedy on French foundations, Wycherley was too base, his metal too tarnished, while Etherege was all flash and no weight, his metal too light to hold value. And beyond them, nothing but the crude British ore of Shadwell’s brutal and boisterous talent remained in circulation.

Taking a metaphor from Landor, we might say that a single limb of Molière would have been enough to forge a Congreve, and a single limb of Congreve would have been enough to forge a Sheridan. Vanbrugh, with his broad and robust humor, carved out comedies so admirable they earn him a place among the masters—though not quite the crown.

His initial foray into comedy was but a refined imitation of models that his own earliest work would ultimately eclipse; and when he turned to tragedy, his handling of it bore the artifice and affectation of Lady Wishfort’s cosmetics—superficially adorned, yet marked by the cracks of inauthenticity. Yet his three seminal comedies alone suffice to establish a legacy as enduring as the language itself. Without them, we would lack exemplars of comedy in its most refined and elevated manifestation. Ben Jonson, the lone figure who sought to reform the theatrical landscape by isolating comedy from the tangled fusion of tragedy and comedy that characterized the stage of his era—a fusion as entwined as life itself—nevertheless failed to imbue his intricate and grand designs with the fluidity and elegance intrinsic to the comic spirit. Among Congreve’s immediate predecessors, who endeavored to construct a new English comedy upon French foundations, Wycherley’s work was of a base alloy, while Etherege’s was too insubstantial to compare. No other contemporaries offered anything beyond the crude, unrefined ore of Shadwell’s coarse and unadorned talent. We call it a singular fact, because we Yankees are thought to be fond of the spread-eagle style, and nothing can be more remote from that than his. We are reckoned a practical folks, who would rather hear about a new air-tight stove than about [Plato](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Author:Plato); yet our favorite teacher's practicality is not in the least of the Poor Richard variety. If he have any Buncombe constituency, it is that unrealized commonwealth of philosophers which Plotinus proposed to establish; and if he were to make an almanac, his directions to farmers would be something like this: "October: *Indian Summer;* now is the time to get in your early Vedas." What, then, is his secret? Is it not that he out-Yankees us all? that his range includes us all? that he is equally at home with the potato-disease and original sin, with pegging shoes and the Over-soul? that, as we try all trades, so has he tried all cultures? and above all, that his mysticism gives us a counterpoise to our super-practicality?

The ancient proverb which declares that love is blind is only a half truth: love is only blind of one eye. The expression "blind hate" also contains only a half truth: hate has one powerful eye. When either of these passions is present, it insatiably sets about discovering new objects to feast upon. The lover collects and broods upon the graces of his beloved from the rising of the lark to the going down of the evening star. The husband who thoroughly loses his temper with his wife at the breakfast table busies himself all day long recollecting and amassing all the grievances that he has felt against her during the last ten years; and he returns at night in a sullen rage and with an almost superhuman insight into the deficiencies of his helpmate. So men of letters set out with gusto and find a relish in every wayside berry; or they set out on the satirical foot with a bad taste in their mouths, and for a whole generation occupy themselves with malicious caricatures of their mistress, Life.

The ancient adage that love is blind reveals only a partial reality: love is blind in one eye, while the other remains piercingly acute. Similarly, the phrase "blind hate" holds only half the truth—hate, though often perceived as sightless, possesses a single, unrelenting eye. When either of these potent emotions takes hold, it consumes itself in an insatiable quest for new objects of fixation. The lover, for instance, accumulates and dwells upon the virtues of the beloved, from the first cry of the lark to the final descent of the evening star. Likewise, a husband who erupts in anger at his wife during breakfast becomes consumed all day with the task of gathering and cataloging grievances, each one a fragment of a decade's worth of resentment. By nightfall, he returns with a sullen fury and an almost superhuman clarity regarding his wife's flaws. Thus, men of letters, with fervor, gather every small detail of their journey, savoring each humble offering of the path; or, with a bitter taste in their mouths, they embark on a satirical pilgrimage, devoting an entire generation to the grotesque exaggeration of their mistress, Life.

When either passion is present, it constantly seeks new objects to focus upon. A lover gathers and dwells on the virtues of his beloved, from the first song of the lark to the setting of the evening star. A husband who loses his temper with his wife at breakfast spends the rest of the day collecting and compiling all the grievances he has felt against her over the past decade. He returns in the evening with a sullen rage and an almost superhuman awareness of his wife's shortcomings. Likewise, men of letters enthusiastically set out and find pleasure in every small detail of their journey; or they begin with a critical mindset, and for an entire generation, they devote themselves to creating malicious caricatures of their mistress, Life.

Writers, too, go out with joy, tasting every small pleasure. Or they go out with bitterness, finding fault in everything and making fun of Life for years.

The old saying that love is blind is but a half-truth: love is blind in one eye, the other sharp and wide as a hawk’s. Likewise, "blind hate" is only half-right—hate has one eye, but it's a cannonball aimed at the heart. When either passion takes hold, it gnaws hungrily at the world, seeking fresh flesh to devour. A lover, for instance, hoards every flicker of grace from the first chirp of the lark to the last sigh of the evening star, turning the day into a shrine. A husband, after a breakfast-table explosion, spends the day dredging up a decade’s worth of slights, until he returns home in a blackened mood, his eyes now surgical, dissecting every flaw in his wife with a surgeon’s precision. Writers, too, set out with ravenous delight, tasting every berry along the path, or they march off with a sour tongue, spending lifetimes drawing twisted portraits of their mistress, Life, in venomous ink.

There was a still more pregnant reason for my desertion of the camp of musical criticism. I seemed always to be about ten years ahead of most of the other critics and the orchestral conductors who make out programs. I missed the reviling of Wagner in New York, but I have watched the pundits of the press revile, in turn, Richard Strauss, Debussy, and Stravinsky, only, in the end, after their ears, through repeated hearings, had grown accustomed to the new clang-tints, to accept these composers as part of the sacred hierarchy. My orchestral education was carried on under Theodore Thomas in Chicago. Now Thomas was not a great conductor, although he always gave honest musical readings of his scores, but he had one great virtue: he believed that new music should be heard. He performed, therefore, every important European composition as soon as possible after it had been performed abroad. As a result, when I arrived in New York in 1906, having listened to and appraised nearly all the major works of Strauss and Debussy composed up to that date, I was amazed to discover that the New York critics were still fighting about these composers, first underpraising them and a little later overpraising them, for Strauss, at any rate, to my mind, has never been a whit superior as a composer to such a man as Liszt. In Paris, in 1913, I heard Stravinsky's [Sacre du Printemps](https://en.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=Sacre_du_Printemps&action=edit&redlink=1) and a good deal more of this Russian's music. I wrote a panegyric about Le Sacre du Printemps in my first book,[[1]](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Red#cite_note-1) published in 1915. In 1924, Le Sacre du Printemps has at last been performed in New York and the critics have at last accepted Stravinsky. So, indeed, apparently, have the conductors who, until the past four years, hardly ever permitted his name to be emblazoned on their programs. The job of music critic in New York, therefore, is certainly not an ideal occupation for a man with imagination and foresight.

There was another, more important reason why I left the world of music criticism. I always seemed to be about ten years ahead of most other critics and the conductors who choose what music to play. I missed the time when people in New York criticized Wagner, but I saw them later criticize Richard Strauss, Debussy, and Stravinsky in turn. At first, they didn't like their music, but after hearing it many times, they came to accept these composers as important figures in music. I studied orchestral music with Theodore Thomas in Chicago. Now, Thomas wasn't a great conductor, but he always played music honestly and with care. His biggest strength was his belief that new music should be heard. He played every major European piece as soon as it was performed elsewhere. Because of that, when I arrived in New York in 1906, I had already heard and formed opinions on nearly all the important works by Strauss and Debussy up to that time. I was surprised to find that the New York critics were still debating these composers, at first underestimating them and then later overestimating them. In my view, Strauss has never been as good a composer as Liszt. In 1913, I heard Stravinsky's *The Rite of Spring* and a lot more of his music in Paris. I wrote a glowing review of *The Rite of Spring* in my first book, published in 1915. In 1924, *The Rite of Spring* was finally performed in New York, and the critics finally accepted Stravinsky. So have the conductors, who until the past few years rarely included his name on their programs. So, the job of a music critic in New York is definitely not a good fit for someone with imagination and the ability to see ahead.

There was a deeper, more weighty reason that drove me from the camp of musical criticism—like a man who, for years, has been sprinting ahead of a slow-moving caravan, only to realize he’s out of sync with the very rhythm of the journey. I found myself perpetually ten years ahead of the critics and conductors who dictated the musical map, their ears tethered to the past, while mine had already wandered into the uncharted territories of the new. I missed the vitriol hurled at Wagner in New York, but I watched, with a mix of bemusement and pity, as the press’s scribes turned their venom upon Strauss, Debussy, and Stravinsky, only to later, through the slow alchemy of repeated listenings, fold these composers into the hallowed pantheon of musical divinity.

My musical training unfolded under the baton of Theodore Thomas in Chicago. Now, Thomas wasn’t a titan of the podium, but his readings were honest, his interpretations unadorned. What he lacked in flash, he made up for in conviction: he believed in the necessity of hearing new music. He gave it a stage, a voice, a place in the concert hall. And so, he brought to Chicago every significant European work as soon as it had been heard across the sea.

By 1906, when I arrived in New York, I had already heard and judged nearly all the major works of Strauss and Debussy up to that point. It struck me as absurd that New York critics were still bickering over them—first dismissing, then lavishing praise upon them. To my ears, Strauss had never climbed above the heights of Liszt. In 1913, in Paris, I heard Stravinsky’s *Sacre du Printemps* and more of his audacious Russian sounds. I penned a hymn to that work in my first book, published in 1915. By 1924, *Le Sacre du Printemps* finally arrived in New York, and the critics, at long last, embraced Stravinsky. Even the conductors, who had previously hidden his name behind the curtains of their programs, now dared to raise it in the light. Thus, it seems, the role of a music critic in New York is no place for a man who dreams and sees ahead.

There was an even more profound rationale for my withdrawal from the camp of musical critique. I often found myself positioned approximately a decade ahead of the majority of critics and orchestral conductors who curate concert programs. I was absent from the vitriolic denunciations of Wagner in New York, yet I observed with interest as the press’s scribes, in succession, turned their scorn toward Richard Strauss, Debussy, and Stravinsky. Eventually, through persistent exposure, their ears acclimated to the novel timbres, and these composers were enshrined within the revered canon. My orchestral education unfolded under Theodore Thomas in Chicago. Though Thomas was not a masterful conductor—his interpretations, while sincere, lacked the transcendent flair of the greats—he possessed a singular virtue: an unwavering conviction that new music must be heard. Consequently, he programmed every significant European composition as soon as it had been performed abroad. Thus, when I arrived in New York in 1906, having already engaged deeply with nearly all the major works of Strauss and Debussy composed up to that point, I was struck by the fact that New York critics were still embroiled in debate over these composers, oscillating between initial disdain and later excessive praise. To my mind, Strauss has never equaled the compositional brilliance of a figure such as Liszt. In Paris, in 1913, I encountered Stravinsky’s *Le Sacre du Printemps* and a substantial portion of his other works. I composed an effusive tribute to *Le Sacre du Printemps* in my first book, published in 1915. By 1924, *Le Sacre du Printemps* had at last reached New York, and the critics had finally embraced Stravinsky. Indeed, the conductors, who for years had scarcely allowed his name to appear on their programs, now seem to have accepted him. Hence, the role of a music critic in New York is certainly not a fitting vocation for one endowed with imagination and foresight.

There was an even more profound rationale for my withdrawal from the camp of musical critique. I often found myself positioned approximately a decade ahead of the majority of critics and orchestral conductors who curate concert programs. I was absent from the vitriolic denunciations of Wagner in New York, yet I observed with interest as the press’s scribes, in succession, turned their scorn toward Richard Strauss, Debussy, and Stravinsky. Eventually, through persistent exposure, their ears acclimated to the novel timbres, and these composers were enshrined within the revered canon. My orchestral education unfolded under Theodore Thomas in Chicago. Though Thomas was not a masterful conductor—his interpretations, while sincere, lacked the transcendent flair of the greats—he possessed a singular virtue: an unwavering conviction that new music must be heard. Consequently, he programmed every significant European composition as soon as it had been performed abroad. Thus, when I arrived in New York in 1906, having already engaged deeply with nearly all the major works of Strauss and Debussy composed up to that point, I was struck by the fact that New York critics were still embroiled in debate over these composers, oscillating between initial disdain and later excessive praise. I composed an effusive tribute to *Le Sacre du Printemps* in my first book, published in 1915. By 1924, *Le Sacre du Printemps* had at last reached New York, and the critics had finally embraced Stravinsky. Indeed, the conductors, who for years had scarcely allowed his name to appear on their programs, now seem to have accepted him. Hence, the role of a music critic in New York is certainly not a fitting vocation for one endowed with imagination and foresight.

First, there was a Teachers' Institute at the county-seat; and there distinguished guests of the superintendent taught the teachers fractions and spelling and other mysteries,—white teachers in the morning, Negroes at night. A picnic now and then, and a supper, and the rough world was softened by laughter and song. I remember how— But I wander. There came a day when all the teachers left the Institute and began the hunt for schools. I learn from hearsay (for my mother was mortally afraid of fire-arms) that the hunting of ducks and bears and men is wonderfully interesting, but I am sure that the man who has never hunted a country school has something to learn of the pleasures of the chase. I see now the white, hot roads lazily rise and fall and wind before me under the burning July sun; I feel the deep weariness of heart and limb as ten, eight, six miles stretch relentlessly ahead; I feel my heart sink heavily as I hear again and again, "Got a teacher? Yes." So I walked on and on—horses were too expensive—until I had wandered beyond railways, beyond stage lines, to a land of "varmints" and rattlesnakes, where the coming of a stranger was an event, and men lived and died in the shadow of one blue hill.

First, a Teachers' Institute bloomed in the county-seat, where the superintendent's guests—distinguished, enigmatic figures—unspooled the secrets of fractions and spelling to the teachers, white ones in the morning, Negroes under the moon’s slow grin. Picnics, suppers, laughter, song—these were the soft edges that bent the rough world into something almost tender. I remember— But I drift. One day, the teachers vanished from the Institute, scattering like startled birds to chase schools. I learned by rumor (my mother, deathly afraid of firearms, never let me near them) that the hunt for ducks, bears, and men was thrilling, but I’m certain the man who’s never stalked a country school misses the thrill of the chase. Now I see those roads—white, blistering, curling like the tongue of the July sun—stretching, rising, falling, winding endlessly. I feel the marrow of my bones ache, my heart a lead weight as mile after mile yawns ahead. "Got a teacher?" "Yes." Again and again, the question, the answer. I walked on—horses were too costly—until I wandered past railways, past stage lines, into a realm of varmints and rattlesnakes, where a stranger’s arrival stirred the whole town, and men lived and died beneath the same blue hill’s brooding gaze.

I feel the marrow of my bones ache, my heart a lead weight as mile after mile yawns ahead. "Got a teacher?" "Yes." Again and again, the question, the answer. I walked on—horses were too costly—until I wandered past railways, past stage lines, into a realm of varmints and rattlesnakes, where a stranger’s arrival stirred the whole town, and men lived and died beneath the same blue hill’s brooding gaze.

Sprinkled over hill and dale lay cabins and farmhouses, shut out from the world by the forests and the rolling hills toward the east. There I found at last a little school. Josie told me of it; she was a thin, homely girl of twenty, with a dark-brown face and thick, hard hair. I had crossed the stream at Watertown, and rested under the great willows; then I had gone to the little cabin in the lot where Josie was resting on her way to town. The gaunt farmer made me welcome, and Josie, hearing my errand, told me anxiously that they wanted a school over the hill; that but once since the war had a teacher been there; that she herself longed to learn,—and thus she ran on, talking fast and loud, with much earnestness and energy.

Scattered like dandelion seeds across the hills and valleys, cabins and farmhouses huddled in the embrace of forests and undulating land to the east. There, nestled in the crook of the world, I stumbled upon a tiny school. Josie had whispered of it—thin, unadorned, twenty years old, her face the color of aged mahogany, her hair a tangle of iron cords. I’d crossed the stream at Watertown, slumped beneath the ancient willows, then trudged to the small cabin where Josie lay recovering from her journey to town. The lanky farmer welcomed me with a nod, and when Josie caught wind of my purpose, she erupted into a flurry of words, eyes alight. She spoke of the school over the hill, how only once since the war had a teacher graced it, how she ached to learn—her voice a storm of passion and urgency.

There is no agency like the home paper for developing a broad human interest and for keeping us in touch with the friendships and the ideals of our youth.

My bands of silk and miniver Momently grew heavier; The black gauze was beggarly thin; The ermine muffled mouth and chin; I could not suck the moonlight in. Harlequin in lozenges Of love and hate, I walked in these Striped and ragged rigmaroles; Along the pavement my footsoles Trod warily on living coals. Shouldering the thoughts I loathed, In their corrupt disguises clothed, Morality I could not tear From my ribs, to leave them bare Ivory in silver air. There I walked, and there I raged; The spiritual savage caged Within my skeleton, raged afresh To feel, behind a carnal mesh, The clean bones crying in the flesh.

My silken bands, embroidered with miniver, grew leaden with time; the black gauze, a beggar's breath, too thin to hold the night. Ermine draped my mouth and chin like a shroud—moonlight, I could not drink. A Harlequin, dressed in lozenges of love and hate, I strode through this patchwork of stripes and rags, my footsoles dancing on coals that hissed beneath. I bore the thoughts I despised, masked in rot and ruse, morality clung to my ribs like ivy, refusing to let go. I walked, I raged—spiritual beast caged in bone, howling through flesh, feeling the clean bones weep beneath the skin.

My silken bands, adorned with miniver, incrementally bore down upon me; the black gauze, meager in its transparency; the ermine, muffling my mouth and chin; I was denied the intake of moonlight. A Harlequin, draped in tessellations of love and hate, I strode through these fragmented, tattered performances; my soles, cautious upon the scorching pavement. Shouldering the thoughts I detested, cloaked in their tawdry guises, I could not extract morality from my ribs, leaving them exposed in the silver air. There I walked, there I raged; the spiritual savage, confined within my skeleton, rekindled its fury, sensing, through a carnal lattice, the pure bones wailing within the flesh.

For God's sake hold your tongue, and let me love, Or chide my palsy, or my gout, My five gray hairs, or ruined fortune flout, With wealth your state, your mind with arts improve, Take you a course, get you a place, Observe his honor, or his grace, Or the king's real, or his stamped face Contemplate; what you will, approve, So you will let me love. Alas, alas, who's injured by my love? What merchant's ships have my sighs drowned? Who says my tears have overflowed his ground? When did my colds a forward spring remove? When did the heats which my veins fill Add one more to the plaguy bill? Soldiers find wars, and lawyers find out still Litigious men, which quarrels move, Though she and I do love. Call us what you will, we are made such by love; Call her one, me another fly, We're tapers too, and at our own cost die,

For the sake of the divine, restrain your speech and permit me to love, or else censure my trembling hands, my aching joints, my five ashen strands, or my despoiled estate. Elevate your station through wealth, refine your intellect through art, pursue a course, secure a position, contemplate the king’s true visage or his emblematic countenance—do what you will, commend it, so long as you allow me to love. Alas, who suffers from my affection? Which merchant’s vessels have been submerged by my sighs? Whose fields have been deluged by my weeping? When did my colds displace the coming spring? When did the fervor within my veins swell the tally of ailments? Warriors seek war, and jurists uncover disputes—yet she and I, though bound by love, are named as such. Call us what you may, we are shaped by love; call her one, me another, we are but tapers, consuming ourselves in our own light.

For the love of heaven, stifle that tongue, and let me love—  
or berate my trembling hands, my gnarled joints,  
my five silver strands, or my shattered coffers,  
dress your soul in wisdom, let your mind bloom with art,  
seek a path, carve a role,  
gaze upon his nobility, his charm,  
or the king’s true face, or the coin’s stamped grin—  
do what you must, endorse it all,  
so long as you let me love.  
Alas, who suffers from my love?  
Which merchant’s vessel has drowned in my sighs?  
Whose fields have been flooded by my weeping?  
When did my chills shift the season’s course?  
When did the fever in my blood  
add a single toll to the cursed ledger?  
War is found by soldiers, quarrels by lawyers,  
yet she and I still love.  
Call us what you will—we are bound by love;  
name her a fly, me another,  
we are tapers too, burning ourselves to ash.

Shall I compare thee to a summers day? Thou art more lovely and more temperate: Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May, And summers lease hath all too short a date; Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines, And often is his gold complexion dimm'd; And every fair from fair sometime declines, By chance or natures changing course untrimm'd; But thy eternal summer shall not fade, Nor lose possession of that fair thou owst; Nor shall death brag thou wanderst in his shade, When in eternal lines to time thou growst: So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.

Would I liken thee to a summer's day? Nay, thou art fairer, more gently kept—rough gusts toss the tender blossoms of May, and summer’s lease is but a fleeting breath; at times the sun’s gaze grows too fierce, and oft its golden face is veiled in gloom; each beauty fades, untrimmed by chance or nature’s fickle turn—yet thy eternal summer shall not wither, nor surrender the grace thou holdest; death shall not boast thee wandering in his shadow, for in endless verse thou shalt outlast time’s cruel tread: so long as breath or sight remains, so long shall this live, and through it, thou shalt live on.

Stella is sick, and in that sick-bed lies Sweetness, that breathes and pants as oft as she; And grace, sick too, such fine conclusions tries That sickness brags itself best graced to be. Beauty is sick, but sick in so fair guise That in that paleness beautys white we see; And joy, which is inseparate from these eyes, Stella now learns (strange case!) to weep in thee. Love moves thy pain, and like a faithful page, As thy looks stir, runs up and down, to make All folks prest at thy will thy pain to assuage; Nature with care sweats for her darlings sake, Knowing worlds pass, ere she enough can find Of such heaven stuff, to clothe so heavenly mind.

Stella lies ailing, and in her fevered bed, Sweetness stirs, breathing in tandem, gasping with her. Grace, too, is unwell, crafting delicate endings that sickness boasts as its finest grace. Beauty, though ill, wears her affliction like a diadem, a pale shimmer that reveals her former radiance. Joy, once inseparable from these eyes, now watches Stella weep—a strange, sorrowful spectacle. Love, your pain is its master, pacing like a loyal scribe, darting to and fro to ease your ache. Nature, in labor, sweats for her darling, knowing entire worlds may crumble before she finds enough celestial stuff to clothe such a divine soul.

Thou art my lute, by thee I sing, My being is attuned to thee. Thou settest all my words a-wing, And meltest me to melody. Thou art my life, by thee I live, From thee proceed the joys I know; Sweetheart, thy hand has power to give The meed of lovethe cup of woe. Thou art my love, by thee I lead My soul the paths of light along, From vale to vale, from mead to mead, And home it in the hills of song. My song, my soul, my life, my all, Why need I pray or make my plea, Since my petition cannot fall; For Im already one with thee!

You are my lute, through you I play, my soul strung tight to your refrain. You launch my words like birds in flight, dissolve me into song. You are my breath, my pulse, my flame—your touch births both the bliss and ache I know. Beloved, your hand pours out the chalice of love, the bitter draught of sorrow. You are my fire, guiding my spirit through sunlit glades and shadowed dells, across meadows, through hills where music dwells. My voice, my heart, my life, my whole—why plead, why pray? For I am already bound to you, fused, fused, fused.

Perspective remains unshaken in their gaze; they uphold the quiet decree of Spring, merging March with the desolate vastness of August's Antarctic expanse. These are creatures whose vision is confined to grass and snow, and the silent core of their existence, unbothered by the transient halo of seasons that may strip them bare, leaving them to wither on the remnants of last year’s stubble. Their movements are clumsy, ponderous, devoid of artifice. We, who operate the cider press, observing them—those of us who sip the sharp, bright bitterness of friendship’s fermented wine, its acidic tang thickening the throat, the slow exchange of grievances (when will we know when the jest has become too cutting to be kind?)—boast of our wealth of trust in others, even as we ourselves might pursue the merriest specter. Above them stands Old Mizzentop, a palatial edifice of white, its floors ascending to dormers crowned with cinquefoil, portholes stacking toward a stoic, unyielding height. Long rows of windows peer outward, toward what once was.

Their eyes, unyielding as the tide, hold fast to perspective, never letting it wither—clinging to Spring’s quiet command, where March’s breath mingles with the hush of August’s Antarctic air. These are not cows who see beyond the green of grass and the white of snow, nor beyond the pulse of their own being, untouched by the golden halo of seasons that pass them by, even as they fade and fall upon last year’s stubble. They lumber, clumsy and uncoy, while we, the cider-pressers, sip our bitter wine of friendship, our tongues numb with the sour tang of promises and shifting grudges—when does the joke become too cruel to be kind? We prattle of our faith in others, yet would ourselves chase down the ghost of mirth. Above them, Old Mizzentop stands, a palace of white, its floors stacked high with dormer portholes, each window a silent sentinel gazing out toward what once was.

Perspective does not fade from their eyes; they maintain that quiet decree of spring, which unites March with the cold skies of August. These are merely cows that perceive nothing beyond grass, snow, and their own internal existence, unbothered by the transient nature of seasons, even as they grow thin and die upon last year's stubble. They are clumsy, heavy, and unrefined. I never knew the earth wore such a crown of gold, the fields spilling it like a drunkard's laugh, this hill—wrinkled, ancient—now a youth ablaze with blossoms that burst and shimmer. What golden storms, what yellow delirium! What a wastrel world, what a generous hand of God! This wood’s edge, a blaze of buttercup and goldrod, a riot of light. You, beloved, are transformed. The fields drink you in, paint you whole… and you stand, a goddess in a world of flame!

Care for thy soul as thing of greatest price, Made to the end to taste of power divine, Devoid of guilt, abhorring sin and vice, Apt by Gods grace to virtue to incline. Care for it so as by thy retchless train It be not brought to taste eternal pain. Care for thy corse, but chiefly for souls sake; Cut off excess, sustaining food is best; To vanquish pride but comely clothing take; Seek after skill, deep ignorance detest. Care so, I say, the flesh to feed and clothe That thou harm not thy soul and body both. Care for the world to do thy body right; Rack not thy wit to win thy wicked ways; Seek not to oppress the weak by wrongful might; To pay thy due do banish all delays. Care to dispend according to thy store, And in like sort be mindful of the poor. Care for thy soul, as for thy chiefest stay; Care for thy body for thy souls avail; Care for the world for bodys help alway; Care yet but so as virtue may prevail. Care in such sort that thou be sure of this: Care keep thee not from heaven and heavenly bliss.

Tend to thy soul as the most precious artifact, forged not for the fleeting pleasures of this world, but to partake in the ineffable essence of the divine, unblemished by transgression, repugnant to moral decay, and predisposed by celestial favor toward the luminous path of virtue. Guard it so that the ceaseless currents of thy actions do not drag it into the abyss of eternal torment. Tend not merely to the cadaver of thy being, but above all to the immortal spark within; curb excess, for moderation is the sustenance of wisdom; shun ostentation, for humility is the truest garment; pursue knowledge, for ignorance is the shadow that devours the soul. Provide for the flesh only in measure, lest thou corrupt both body and spirit. Attend to the world not for self-aggrandizement, but for the integrity of thy frame; do not exhaust thy mind in the pursuit of vice; do not subjugate the vulnerable through unjust dominion; discharge thy obligations without delay. Spend according to thy means, yet remember the destitute. Cherish the soul as thy ultimate anchor, the body as a vessel for the soul's ascent, and the world as a means to sustain the body's function—all in such a manner that virtue remains sovereign. Let thy care be so directed that thou art certain of this: that thy care does not bar thee from the gates of heaven and the embrace of celestial felicity.

Take care of your soul, for it is the most valuable thing. It was made to experience the power of God, free from guilt and hatred of sin, and ready to turn to goodness through God's grace. Keep it safe so it does not suffer eternal pain. Take care of your body, but mainly for the sake of your soul. Eat enough but not too much, and dress modestly to fight pride. Learn and avoid ignorance. Take care of your body so you do not harm your soul or your body. Take care of the world by treating your body well, but do not use your mind to do evil. Do not oppress the weak. Pay what you owe and do not delay. Spend wisely and remember the poor. Take care of your soul, for it is your main support. Take care of your body to help your soul. Take care of the world to help your body, but always in a way that goodness wins. Take care in such a way that you can be certain this is true: caring will not keep you from heaven or the joy of heaven.

Care for your soul as the most valuable possession, created for the purpose of experiencing divine power, free from guilt, rejecting sin and vice, and inclined by divine grace toward virtue. Ensure that through your actions, your soul does not suffer eternal pain. While you should care for your body, your primary concern must be for your soul. Avoid excess, and consume only what is necessary; reject pride by limiting your clothing to what is appropriate; pursue knowledge and avoid ignorance. Provide for your body and clothe it in a manner that does not harm your soul or your physical being. Take care of your body for the benefit of your soul, and care for the world to support your body. Do not strain your mind to pursue wicked behavior; do not oppress the weak through unjust power; fulfill your obligations without delay. Spend according to your means, and be mindful of the poor. Care for your soul as your greatest support, care for your body for the benefit of your soul, and care for the world for the sake of your body. However, ensure that your care is guided by virtue, so that you may be assured of a place in heaven and eternal happiness.

Tend to thy soul as the most precious artifact, forged not for the fleeting pleasures of this world, but to partake in the ineffable essence of the divine, unblemished by transgression, repugnant to moral decay, and predisposed by celestial favor toward the luminous path of virtue. Guard it so that the ceaseless currents of thy actions do not drag it into the abyss of eternal torment. Tend not merely to the cadaver of thy being, but above all to the immortal spark within; curb excess, for moderation is the sustenance of wisdom; shun ostentation, for humility is the truest garment; pursue knowledge, for ignorance is the shadow that devours the soul. Provide for the flesh only in measure, lest thou corrupt both body and spirit. Attend to the world not for self-aggrandizement, but for the integrity of thy frame; do not exhaust thy mind in the pursuit of vice; do not subjugate the vulnerable through unjust dominion; discharge thy obligations without delay. Spend according to thy means, yet remember the destitute. Cherish the soul as thy ultimate anchor, the body as a vessel for the soul's ascent, and the world as a means to sustain the body's function—all in such a manner that virtue remains sovereign. Let thy care be so directed that thou art certain of this: that thy care does not bar thee from the gates of heaven and the embrace of celestial felicity.

Tend to thy soul as if it were a jewel spun from starlight, forged not for the mundane but to sip from the chalice of the divine, unblemished by sin's black stain, yearning to be shaped by grace into a vessel of virtue. Guard it fiercely, lest thy daily deeds, hollow and heedless, drag it into the abyss of endless torment. Tend to thy body, yes, but only as a servant to the soul's grand design—cut back on indulgence, feed with measured hands; let modesty in dress curb pride's swelling tide. Pursue wisdom, shun the fog of ignorance. Nurture both flesh and spirit with care, lest one devour the other. Tend to the world, but not with twisted ambition; let not thy mind be a forge for vice. Release the weak from thy grip, and pay thy debts without delay. Spend thy wealth with wisdom, and never forget the poor. Tend to thy soul as thy anchor, thy body as its shield, the world as its ally—but always, always, let virtue be the compass. Do this, and thou shalt find thyself not barred from the gates of heaven, but cradled in its eternal light.

Time only cause of my unrest By whom I hopd once to bee blest How cruell art thou turned? That first gavst lyfe unto my love, And still a pleasure nott to move Or change though ever burned; Have I thee slackd, or left undun One loving rite, and soe have wunn Thy rage or bitter changing? That now noe minutes I shall see, Wherein I may least happy bee Thy favors soe estranging. Blame thy self, and nott my folly, Time gave time butt to bee holly; True love such ends best loveth Unworhty love doth seeke for ends A worthy love butt worth pretends Nor other thoughts itt proveth: Then stay thy swiftnes cruell time, And lett mee once more blessed clime To joy, that I may prayse thee: Lett mee pleasure sweetly tasting Joy in love, and faith nott wasting And on fames wings Ile rayse thee: Never shall thy glory dying Bee untill thine owne untying That time noe longer liveth; Tis a gaine such tyme to lend: Since soe thy fame shall never end Butt joy for what she giveth.

Time, the thief of my calm, the bringer of my unrest—  
Once I leapt, hopeful, toward your blessing,  
Now I curse the cruel twist you've taken!  
You, who first gave breath to my love,  
Yet keep it locked in stillness,  
A pleasure that never moves, never shifts,  
Though it burns, it burns in silence.  
Have I, by slackness or neglect,  
Broken any vow of love?  
Have I earned your wrath, your bitter turn?  
Now, in every minute, I find no peace,  
No moment free from your cold favor.  
Blame not my folly, but yourself—  
Time gave you time to be whole,  
True love ends best,  
Unworthy love seeks only ends.  
Stay, cruel time, and let me taste joy once more,  
Let me bask in love's sweet pleasure,  
Let me raise you on wings of fame—  
Your glory shall never fade,  
Not until time itself ceases to live.  
What a gain, to lend you such time:  
For your fame shall never end,  
But flourish in the joy you give.

Time is the sole cause of my unrest. I once hoped to be blessed by it. How cruel you have become? You first gave life to my love, and yet you do not move or change, even as it burns. Have I neglected any loving duty or failed in any rite, thereby inviting your wrath or altering your favor? Now, in every moment, I find myself least happy, as your favor grows distant. Blame yourself, not my folly. Time grants time only to be holy. True love accepts such an end best; unworthy love seeks only ends, while worthy love merely pretends to be worth it, proving no other thoughts. Therefore, stop, cruel time, and allow me once more to experience blessed joy, so I may praise you. Let me taste pleasure, find joy in love, and not waste faith. On the wings of fame, I shall elevate you. Your glory shall never fade until time itself ceases to live. It is a gain to grant such time, for your fame shall never end, but only joy for what it gives.

Time, the sole architect of my disquiet, by whose hands I once aspired to be blessed—how cruelly have you transformed? You, who first bestowed life upon my love, yet now persist in a pleasure that neither stirs nor shifts, though ever burning. Have I neglected you, or forsaken any sacred act of devotion, thus provoking your wrath or bitter metamorphosis? Now, in no moment shall I find respite from your favor’s estrangement. Blame not my folly, but yourself—time granted time only to be holy; true love finds its end in devotion, while unworthy love seeks closure. A worthy love merely feigns value, proving no other intent. Cease, then, your cruel swiftness, O time, and allow me once again to ascend to blessed realms of joy, that I may laud you. Let me taste sweet pleasure, experience love’s joy, and preserve faith, not squandered. On fame’s wings I shall elevate you: never shall your glory fade until time itself ceases to live. Thus, to lend you such time is gain, for your fame shall never end, but endure as joy for what she gives.

Sweet shades why doe you seeke to give delight To mee who deeme delight in this vilde place Butt torment, sorrow, and mine owne disgrace To taste of joy, or your vaine pleasing sight; Show them your pleasures who saw never night Of greife, wher joyings fauning, smiling face Appeers as day, wher griefe found never space Yett for a sigh, a grone, or envies spite; Butt O on mee a world of woes doe ly, Or els on mee all harmes strive to rely, And to attend like servants bound to mee, Heat in desire, while frosts of care I prove, Wanting my love, yett surfett doe with love Burne, and yett freeze, better in hell to bee.

Sweet shadows, why do you strain to cast delight upon me, who find no joy but anguish in this cursed place? To me, your fleeting pleasures taste only of torment, sorrow, and my own disgrace. Let those who have never known the night of grief behold your smiling faces, bright as day, while I endure the frost of care. Yet upon me lies a world of woe, or all misfortune conspires to cling. Like servants bound to me, desire burns hot, while care's frost chills me. I lack love, yet drown in it—scorching, freezing, better to be damned in hell.

O shadowed specters, why do you strive to bestow delight upon me, who find in this desolate realm only anguish, sorrow, and my own ignominy? Let those who have never known the night of grief behold your fleeting pleasures, where joy's counterfeit visage shines like day. To me, the sighs, the groans, the stings of envy are but the burdens I bear. A universe of woe lies upon me, or all misfortunes conspire to dwell within me, their attendants bound in servitude. I burn with longing, yet freeze beneath the frost of care; I lack love, yet am glutted with it, tormented by the paradox, and would rather dwell in hell.

Sweet shades, why do you seek to give delight To me who deem delight in this vile place But torment, sorrow, and my own disgrace? To taste of joy, or your vain pleasing sight; Show them your pleasures who saw never night Of grief, where joyings, fauning, smiling face Appears as day, where grief found never space Yet for a sigh, a groan, or envies spite; But O, on me a world of woes do lie, Or else on me all harms strive to rely, And to attend like servants bound to me, Heat in desire, while frosts of care I prove, Wanting my love, yet surfeit do with love Burne, and yet freeze; better in hell to be.

Whoso list to hunt, I know where is an hind, But as for me, helas, I may no more. The vain travail hath wearied me so sore, I am of them that farthest cometh behind. Yet may I by no means my wearied mind Draw from the deer, but as she fleeth afore Fainting I follow. I leave off therefore, Sithens in a net I seek to hold the wind. Who list her hunt, I put him out of doubt, As well as I may spend his time in vain. And graven with diamonds in letters plain There is written, her fair neck round about: Noli me tangere, for Caesar's I am, And wild for to hold, though I seem tame.

Whosoever seeks to pursue, I know the location of the hind, yet for myself, alas, I can no longer proceed. The futile exertion has so utterly exhausted me that I lag farthest behind the rest. Still, I cannot disengage my weary mind from the chase, for as she flees ahead, I falter in her wake. Therefore, I abandon the pursuit, since to ensnare the wind within a net is an exercise in futility. To those who wish to pursue her, I relinquish them to doubt, for their efforts shall be spent in vain. Inscribed in plain letters, carved in diamonds upon her fair neck, it reads: *Noli me tangere*, for I belong to Caesar, and though I appear tame, I am untamable in spirit.

My true-love hath my heart and I have his, By just exchange one for the other given: I hold his dear, and mine he cannot miss; There never was a bargain better driven. His heart in me keeps me and him in one; My heart in him his thoughts and senses guides: He loves my heart, for once it was his own; I cherish his because in me it bides. His heart his wound received from my sight; My heart was wounded with his wounded heart; For as from me on him his hurt did light, So still, methought, in me his hurt did smart: Both equal hurt, in this change sought our bliss, My true love hath my heart and I have his.

My true-love possesses my heart, and I possess his, an equitable exchange, each giving what they received: I value his, and he cannot lack mine; no transaction was ever more deftly executed. His heart within me binds us into one; my heart within him steers his thoughts and perceptions. He loves my heart, for once it belonged to him; I cherish his, for it resides in me. His heart bore a wound from my gaze; my heart was wounded by his wounded heart. As his injury was kindled by my presence, so too does his pain dwell within me, a reciprocal ache. Equal suffering, through this metamorphosis, became our felicity: my true-love possesses my heart, and I possess his.

Walking the fields a wantcatcher I spied, To him I went, desirous of his game: Sir, have you taken wants? Yes, he replied, Here are a dozen, which were lately taen. Then you have left no more. No more? quoth he. Sir I can show you more: the more the worse; And to his work he went, but 'twould not be, For all the wants were crept into my purse. Farewell friend wantcatcher, since 'twill not be, Thou cannot catch the wants, but they catch me.

Farewell, wantcatcher, for it won’t be—thou canst not catch wants, but they catch me.

Now in the West the slender moon lies low, And now Orion glimmers through the trees, Clearing the earth with even pace and slow, And now the stately-moving Pleiades, In that soft infinite darkness overhead Hang jewel-wise upon a silver thread. And all the lonelier stars that have their place, Calm lamps within the distant southern sky, And planet-dust upon the edge of space, Look down upon the fretful world, and I Look up to outer vastness unafraid And see the stars which sang when earth was made.

Now the West cradles a thin, pale moon, slung low like a silver sliver in the night's grip, while Orion flickers through the trees, a hunter's ghost in the dark. Slow and sure, he clears the earth with each measured step. The Pleiades drift, regal and stately, strung like jewels on a celestial thread, hanging in the soft, bottomless dark above. Far off, the southern sky holds its calm lamps, distant stars and planet-dust at space’s edge. They peer down on this restless world, and I, unafraid, lift my gaze to the endless void, where stars sing of the day the earth was born.

Potuia, potuia White grave goddess, Pity my sadness, O silence of Paros. I am not of these about thy feet, These garments and decorum; I am thy brother, Thy lover of aforetime crying to thee, And thou hearest me not. I have whispered thee in thy solitudes Of our loves in Phrygia, The far ecstasy of burning noons When the fragile pipes Ceased in the cypress shade, And the brown fingers of the shepherd Moved over slim shoulders; And only the cicada sang. I have told thee of the hills And the lisp of reeds And the sun upon thy breasts, And thou hearest me not, Potuia, potuia Thou hearest me not.

Potuia, potuia—White grave goddess, let your pity fall on my sorrow, O silence of Paros. I do not tread these paths where others linger, wrapped in their finery and decorum. I am not a stranger, but thy brother, thy lover from a time long gone, weeping now to thee, yet thou dost not hear. I have murmured to thee in thy lonely halls of memory, of our loves in Phrygia, of the wild rapture of suns that scorched the sky. When the reeds grew still in cypress shade, when the shepherd’s brown hands traced the curves of your youth, and only the cicada’s song remained. I have spoken of hills, of reeds whispering secrets, of sunlit skin, yet still, Potuia, potuia, thou hearest me not.

I am not a stranger, but thy brother, thy lover from a time long gone, weeping now to thee, yet thou dost not hear. I have murmured to thee in thy lonely halls of memory, of our loves in Phrygia, of the wild rapture of suns that scorched the sky. When the reeds grew still in cypress shade, when the shepherd’s brown hands traced the curves of your youth, and only the cicada’s song remained. I have spoken of hills, of reeds whispering secrets, of sunlit skin, yet still, Potuia, potuia, thou hearest me not.
